Economic Scenarios, Expectations Gaps, and Measuring AI Pace

Anthropic News · Landscape & Orientation · gap-fill/anthropic-news/economic-scenarios-expectations-and-pace.md

Debates about AI’s future often mix three different questions: what the economy does if capabilities unfold a certain way, what people believe will happen, and how fast labs are actually automating their own R&D. Anth…

articlecorpus/anthropic-newscluster/landscape-orientationgap-fill

Keywords: ai-development-timeline, anthropic-news, landscape-orientation, cluster-landscape-orientation, corpus-anthropic-news, article, gap-fill, economic, scenarios, expectations, gaps, measuring, pace

Related: AI Development Timeline

Debates about AI’s future often mix three different questions: what the economy does if capabilities unfold a certain way, what people believe will happen, and how fast labs are actually automating their own R&D. Anthropic Institute and research pieces separate those layers.

Scenario models: map beliefs to outcomes

Economic scenario explorers translate assumptions—automation vs augmentation, productivity uplift, adoption speed, new task creation—into paths for GDP, wages, and unemployment. In moderate growth worlds, unemployment can stay historically familiar while wages vary by industry. In historically unprecedented growth worlds, knowledge-worker wages and job prospects can suffer even as society gets much richer—making distribution the central policy problem.

The teaching use: force explicit inputs. “AI will be transformative” is not a forecast until you state capability, adoption, and task mix.

The expectations gap

Surveys comparing the general public (and AI-using workers) to frontier-lab staff show systematic gaps:

  • Both groups expect rapid capability gains; staff expect faster progress (e.g. far higher shares expecting Nobel-level discovery by a near horizon).
  • Staff report larger time savings on AI-suitable tasks and expect AI to cover most of their own jobs sooner than typical workers expect for theirs.
  • Despite different capability beliefs, both groups link “AI does more of my job” to higher unemployment expectations similarly.

So disagreement about economic impact is not only vibes about “jobs”—it is partly who sits closest to the capability curve, plus a shared mental model connecting personal automation to labor markets.

Measuring pace inside the lab

Capability evals say what models can do. Pace metrics say how models are built:

  1. AI-led AI R&D — how much of the next model is built by AI vs humans.
  2. Oversight of agents — ability to monitor and interrupt agents acting on lab systems.
  3. Compute allocation — resources flowing into more capable models.

Publishing snapshots (and inviting embedded evaluators to verify) gives governments and the public instruments for “pace the frontier” debates that are otherwise opaque. These metrics are complements to RSP-style risk reports, not replacements.

Connecting the dots across the gap-fill corpus

This article sits in a multi-source teaching set. Cross-link it when you teach:

  • Compute and factories (Epoch chip geography, NVIDIA DSX/recovery/cooling) when the bottleneck is physical capacity, power, or utilization rather than model cleverness.
  • Agents and harnesses (Anthropic sandboxes, NVIDIA NeMo failure loops, OpenShell/Sentry) when the bottleneck is tool privilege, traces, or runtime policy.
  • Governance and privacy (CSET actor maps, FPF ADM/chatbot/biometric drafts, Google contextual agent privacy) when the bottleneck is legal scope, preemption, or appropriate information flow.
  • Science and integrity (Epoch acknowledgment trends, Spectrum AI-slop, Google Chain-of-Evidence, wet-lab grounding) when the bottleneck is evidence, disclosure, or physical verification.

Assign one cross-folder compare-and-contrast: same concept, two source cultures (lab blog vs policy center vs engineering journalism). Students should leave able to explain why the framings differ—not only recite facts from one page.

Common misconceptions to correct early

Students often conflate adjacent ideas that this article carefully separates. Correct these early:

  • Capability ≠ deployment. A strong score, demo, or RFP does not prove fielded systems, legal compliance, or safe operations.
  • Openness ≠ safety or soft power by itself. Weights, licenses, orchestration, and compute access each change the influence and risk story differently.
  • Human-in-the-loop ≠ meaningful control when volume, latency, or rubber-stamping hollow out review.
  • Security transforms ≠ category exits in privacy law: a one-way template can still identify; a sandbox can still be misconfigured.
  • Foundation models ≠ finished products in health, Earth, or science: adaptation, thresholds, escalation, and evidence chains remain the product.

Ask learners to spot which misconception a headline is exploiting, then rewrite the headline with the distinction restored.

Takeaways

  • Separate scenario mechanics, belief surveys, and production-process metrics—they answer different questions.
  • Lab-vs-public expectation gaps are data, not noise; use them when interpreting pundit disagreement.
  • If pacing policy matters, demand measurable R&D automation and oversight—not only leaderboard charts.

China’s AI Governance Proposals: Who Holds Which Duties?

CSET Georgetown · Landscape & Orientation · gap-fill/cset-georgetown/china-ai-governance-actors.md

China was early to regulate recommendation algorithms (2021) and frames AI as a major strategic opportunity toward world leadership by 2030. CSET’s comparative read of five major Chinese AI governance proposals (2016–…

articlecorpus/cset-georgetowncluster/landscape-orientationgap-fill

Keywords: ai-development-timeline, cset-georgetown, landscape-orientation, cluster-landscape-orientation, corpus-cset-georgetown, article, gap-fill, china, governance, proposals, holds, which, duties

Related: AI Development Timeline

China was early to regulate recommendation algorithms (2021) and frames AI as a major strategic opportunity toward world leadership by 2030. CSET’s comparative read of five major Chinese AI governance proposals (2016–2024) focuses less on slogans and more on which actors get which responsibilities—the machinery that makes governance real. The finding that travels: older proposals often lack clarity about who governs what; newer ones name actors and assign detailed duties.

Why actor maps beat principle lists

Principles language (“safe,” “controllable,” “people-centered”) travels easily across regimes. Implementation does not. Hipolito Calero’s CSET analysis treats named ministries, regulators, industry bodies, local governments, and enterprises as the unit of analysis because duties without owners are theater. For outsiders reading translations, the checklist is:

  • Which body owns licensing, content controls, safety evaluation, or standards-setting?
  • Are local governments implementers, experimenters, or both?
  • How do enterprise duties (model providers, platforms, algorithm operators) interact with state agencies?
  • Do proposals create overlapping jurisdictions—a predictable friction point when multiple agencies claim the same lifecycle stage?

Dating each proposal matters: China’s AI governance landscape moved from broad strategy documents toward more operational role assignment. Comparative work that ignores dates will invent false continuity.

Government model-use guidelines as a concrete case

A related CSET translation of Guidelines for Deployment and Application of AI Large Models in the Government Sector (internet/cybersecurity regulator guidance) shows the implementer view rather than the international messaging view. The guidance encourages government offices to use AI to speed paperwork, improve surveillance effectiveness, and help predict events such as market swings or disasters—while warning against ad-hoc adoption and urging lower levels to align with systems chosen higher up. It does not pick vendors; it regulates how government may deploy. Hierarchical consistency and risk aversion sit beside efficiency ambitions.

That pairing is pedagogically useful: China’s “governance” includes both market/product controls (algorithms, generative content) and state self-discipline about how agencies adopt models.

Separate strategy from use controls

Teach three layers that often get collapsed in commentary:

  1. Development strategy — catch up / lead by 2030; industrial and compute goals.
  2. Use controls — recommendation algorithms, deep synthesis, generative AI content rules.
  3. Government deployment rules — how public bodies may procure and run large models.

Actor specificity can rise in layer (2) and (3) even while layer (1) stays slogan-heavy. Analysts who only quote the 2017 New Generation AI Development Plan will miss the later machinery.

How to teach this carefully

  • Prefer organizational charts and obligation lists over preamble poetry.
  • Treat translations and secondary analyses as inputs; cite Chinese originals when making legal claims.
  • Expect revision: actor maps are snapshots, not constitutions.
  • Compare with EU/US debates: China often regulates deployed systems and platforms early; Western debates sometimes fixate on frontier labs alone.

Classroom and practice checklist

Use this piece as a concept explainer, not a news brief. When teaching or briefing:

  • Restate the core mechanism in one sentence before citing any organization or product name.
  • Separate what is measured from what is claimed—numbers, thresholds, and evaluation designs are the durable content.
  • Map at least one failure mode (silent fallback, overclaim, approval fatigue, distribution shift, or missing evidence chain).
  • Name the operator decision the idea changes: release gating, procurement, curriculum design, facility build, or legal scope.
  • Leave students with a verification habit: which primary source, diagnostic, or audit would falsify the headline?

These habits travel across geopolitics, privacy law, compute economics, agent harnesses, and applied science stacks alike.

Takeaways

  • Governance capacity is visible in assigned responsibilities, not preamble text.
  • Recent Chinese proposals trend toward specificity of actors—that is the signal to track.
  • Government deployment guides reveal state priorities: efficiency, prediction, hierarchical consistency.
  • Overlapping jurisdictions are a feature to analyze, not noise to ignore.

Sources

  • An Analysis of China’s AI Governance Proposals
  • Guidelines for the Deployment and Application of Artificial Intelligence Large Models in the Government Sector

EU AI Code of Practice: Systemic Risk as a Process

CSET Georgetown · Landscape & Orientation · gap-fill/cset-georgetown/eu-ai-code-of-practice-safety.md

The EU’s AI regulatory stack pairs binding rules with a voluntary Code of Practice that operationalizes how general-purpose AI (GPAI) providers should handle systemic risk. CSET’s July 2025 analysis of the Safety and…

articlecorpus/cset-georgetowncluster/landscape-orientationgap-fill

Keywords: ai-development-timeline, cset-georgetown, landscape-orientation, cluster-landscape-orientation, corpus-cset-georgetown, article, gap-fill, code, practice, systemic, risk, process

Related: AI Development Timeline

The EU’s AI regulatory stack pairs binding rules with a voluntary Code of Practice that operationalizes how general-purpose AI (GPAI) providers should handle systemic risk. CSET’s July 2025 analysis of the Safety and Security chapter treats compliance as a continuous loop—not a one-time checklist—and asks whether the Code could become a de facto global template.

Where the Code sits in the AI Act

The AI Act requires advanced-model providers to mitigate risks; Articles 53 and 55 obligations for GPAI (and systemic-risk GPAI) needed operational detail. The Commission’s three Code chapters—transparency, copyright, and safety/security—supply that detail. GPAI thresholds cited in CSET’s walkthrough include training compute above 10^23 FLOPs for transparency/copyright duties and above 10^25 FLOPs for systemic-risk safety duties (capturing well-known frontier models). Adherence is voluntary, but presumption of conformity is a strong incentive: regulators may treat Code adherence as demonstrating Act compliance, cutting administrative burden versus bespoke proof.

Identify → evaluate → estimate → gate release

The safety chapter addresses Article 55(1) obligations by defining a risk-management process that runs whenever major deployment decisions happen—new systemic-risk GPAI market entry or significant updates. Providers must:

  • Identify potential systemic risks using literature, training-data analysis, incident databases, and expert/lay input.
  • Analyze and evaluate with state-of-the-art methods (benchmarks, red teaming, human-uplift studies) aimed at each risk.
  • Build risk scenarios for how harms could unfold post-deployment.
  • Feed findings into risk estimation (likelihood × severity) and compare against pre-defined, measurable acceptance criteria tied to capabilities.
  • Mitigate and repeat until residual risk is acceptable across identified risks—then release.

Steps are interconnected: modeling informs eval design; post-market monitoring and independent expertise feed back into analysis. Pre-commitment to thresholds is the anti-rationalization mechanism—teams should not quietly raise tolerance at ship time.

Lifecycle governance, not a launch PDF

Beyond the pre-release loop, the Code stresses ongoing light-touch evaluations, mitigations, post-market monitoring, incident reporting, and internal accountability structures. CSET’s teaching angle: the chapter sets a minimum standard of practice that can exceed ad-hoc industry custom if widely adopted. Global impact may resemble GDPR’s pull—providers serving the EU market standardize processes elsewhere for cost and reputation.

Companion CSET work on AI governance at the frontier reminds readers that proposals elsewhere still disagree on oversight actors and which risk techniques work; the EU Code is one operational answer, not the only possible one.

Classroom and practice checklist

Use this piece as a concept explainer, not a news brief. When teaching or briefing:

  • Restate the core mechanism in one sentence before citing any organization or product name.
  • Separate what is measured from what is claimed—numbers, thresholds, and evaluation designs are the durable content.
  • Map at least one failure mode (silent fallback, overclaim, approval fatigue, distribution shift, or missing evidence chain).
  • Name the operator decision the idea changes: release gating, procurement, curriculum design, facility build, or legal scope.
  • Leave students with a verification habit: which primary source, diagnostic, or audit would falsify the headline?

These habits travel across geopolitics, privacy law, compute economics, agent harnesses, and applied science stacks alike.

Builder implication

If you ship GPAI into the EU, treat the Code as a product requirements document for evidence: which evals, which residual-risk narratives, which incident channels. Pair it with the binding Act calendar in ../global-policy/eu-ai-act-risk-based-rules.md—the Code does not replace EUR-Lex obligations; it operationalizes how providers argue conformity.

Takeaways

  • Systemic-risk compliance is a feedback loop, not a single red-team weekend.
  • Presumption of conformity makes a “voluntary” code strategically sticky.
  • Pre-defined acceptance tiers are the governance innovation to watch for diffusion.
  • Continuous monitoring and incident reporting are part of the safety claim, not footnotes.

Sources

  • AI Governance at the Frontier
  • EUR-Lex — Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act)

Open Models as Soft Power in US–China Competition

Weights that anyone can download are not only a research norm—they are a geostrategic distribution channel. CSET/RAND analysis (*Open Models, Soft Power, and the Spectrum of U.S.-China Artificial Intelligence Competit…

Keywords: ai-development-timeline, open-weight-soft-power, cset-georgetown, landscape-orientation, cluster-landscape-orientation, corpus-cset-georgetown, article, gap-fill, open, models, soft, power, china, competition

Related: AI Development Timeline, Open-Weight Soft Power

Weights that anyone can download are not only a research norm—they are a geostrategic distribution channel. CSET/RAND analysis (Open Models, Soft Power, and the Spectrum of U.S.-China Artificial Intelligence Competition, March 2026) argues the open-model ecosystem is becoming a primary arena for influence: who sets defaults for developers worldwide may matter as much as who trains the single best closed model. National security remains one dimension; markets, standards, and stack lock-in are others.

Soft power, defined for AI stacks

Soft power here means shaping others’ preferences through ideology, commercial opportunity, and attractiveness—not only military strength. Broad adoption of one country’s open models can lock researchers and startups into that country’s tooling, licenses, cloud, and norms, especially across the Global South where compute budgets and vendor choice are constrained. “Open” is therefore an export strategy as much as a research culture.

Diverging plan language

The paper contrasts action-plan rhetoric:

  • US AI Action Plan — Create a supportive environment for open models (compute access, partnerships, SME adoption) so leading open models reflect American values and become commercial/academic standards—while still leaving release choices to developers and tying openness to exporting the wider US stack (hardware, models, software, applications, standards).
  • China’s Global AI Governance Action Plan — Stresses transnational open-source communities, lower barriers, Global South access, and UN-centered cooperation—while language about avoiding “duplication of investment” also reads as a push to entrench Chinese platforms and standards.

China’s earlier (2017) development plan already treated open AI as an innovation pathway; 2025 releases such as DeepSeek R1 and Moonshot Kimi K2 made highly capable Chinese open weights globally salient. Perception matters: if the US is seen as closed-by-default and China as the sharer, soft power accrues regardless of raw MMLU deltas.

Policy levers the analysis emphasizes

Authors recommend stronger US support for a healthy open-model ecosystem; recalibration of export controls where they conflict with legitimate open diffusion; and incentives for permissive licensing. The strategic aim is preventing a world where China is perceived as the primary champion of shared AI benefits while US policy accidentally cedes the developer default layer.

How to score “open” in competition analysis

  • Track downloads, derivatives, and regional adoption, not only peak closed-model evals.
  • Separate weights availability from ecosystem gravity (tooling, docs, hosting, licenses).
  • Read governance plans as stack-export strategies with openness as marketing and mechanism.
  • Watch whether export-control design accidentally starves allied open ecosystems.

Classroom and practice checklist

Use this piece as a concept explainer, not a news brief. When teaching or briefing:

  • Restate the core mechanism in one sentence before citing any organization or product name.
  • Separate what is measured from what is claimed—numbers, thresholds, and evaluation designs are the durable content.
  • Map at least one failure mode (silent fallback, overclaim, approval fatigue, distribution shift, or missing evidence chain).
  • Name the operator decision the idea changes: release gating, procurement, curriculum design, facility build, or legal scope.
  • Leave students with a verification habit: which primary source, diagnostic, or audit would falsify the headline?

These habits travel across geopolitics, privacy law, compute economics, agent harnesses, and applied science stacks alike.

Builder implication

Open weights change who can fine-tune and redistribute, not who owns the best closed API on day one. For product strategy, track license terms, data/compute access for downstream builders, and month-scale catch-up on capability indices (see ../epoch-ai/open-vs-closed-cyber-gap.md and ../market-players/open-weight-ecosystems-and-soft-power.md). Soft power is an adoption story: ecosystems win when defaults stick.

Takeaways

  • Open releases are soft-power instruments when they set defaults and lock-in.
  • Compare US and Chinese plans on openness claims vs platform entrenchment.
  • Soft power fails if weights exist but developers cannot access compute or permissive licenses.
  • Competition literacy requires adoption maps alongside leaderboard charts.

In March 2026 the White House released a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence—legislative recommendations for Congress, not just another strategy memo. CSET’s unpacking piece stresses the genre differ…

articlecorpus/cset-georgetowncluster/landscape-orientationgap-fill

Keywords: ai-development-timeline, global-ai-policy-regimes, cset-georgetown, landscape-orientation, cluster-landscape-orientation, corpus-cset-georgetown, article, gap-fill, unpacking, national, policy, framework

Related: AI Development Timeline, Global AI Policy Regimes

In March 2026 the White House released a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence—legislative recommendations for Congress, not just another strategy memo. CSET’s unpacking piece stresses the genre difference: prior documents (July 2025 AI Action Plan, executive orders) set direction; this framework names statutes Congress should pass to match administration goals. It is non-binding, contains no self-executing executive directives, and varies widely in specificity.

Why it exists: preemption after failed moratoria

The framework follows the December 2025 executive order directing advisors to prepare a uniform federal AI policy after Congress repeatedly failed to enact a state-AI-law moratorium (including attempts to condition federal funds on non-enforcement). The political project is clear: preempt fragmented state AI rules and assert federal leadership aligned with the administration’s agenda. CSET reads the document as an opening move in negotiation with Congress—not a finished regime.

What the framework signals (and what it leaves open)

Compared with the Action Plan’s agency-heavy focus, the framework mixes innovation/energy priorities with issues that already move statehouses and polls:

  • Child safety / parental empowerment appears more prominently than in prior Trump-era AI strategy—likely acknowledgment of bipartisan chatbot and youth-protection bills.
  • Censorship / free speech / “ideological bias” language continues themes from earlier executive orders, including efforts to future-proof content priorities against later administrations.
  • Deepfakes and identity misuse get commercial and IP framing, with carveouts for parody/satire that will be hard to operationalize; unlike the child-safety section, deepfake discussion does not clearly protect existing state laws from preemption.
  • Innovation sandboxes, federal dataset readiness, and sector-specific existing authorities appear without detailed implementation recipes.
  • Frontier catastrophic risk is lightly treated—agencies should “understand and plan”—consistent with a light-touch innovation posture.

Section VII’s preemption categories are especially broad: states should not govern (1) AI development, (2) use of AI for activity that would be lawful without AI, and (3) developer liability for unlawful third-party conduct. CSET flags the ambiguity—does (2) block employment/health AI rules, or only prevent AI-specific safety duties?—and notes the administration may prefer Congress to ban state action without filling the federal gap.

Congress as the real arena

Two days before the White House release, Senator Blackburn floated a TRUMP AI AMERICA Act discussion draft with overlapping child/creator themes but different preemption design (conflict preemption vs categorical state abstention) and contested extras such as Section 230 sunset and developer duties of care. Alignment is partial; industry pushback and interstate politics will decide what survives. Midterm pressure may favor “low-hanging fruit” such as workforce-task tracking and agency technical capacity—even if preemption remains toxic on both aisles.

How to teach the document

  • Distinguish strategy docs, executive orders, and legislative frameworks.
  • Track preemption fights as seriously as “AI safety” substance—they are the US governance drama.
  • Read section menus as bargaining chips, not enacted law.
  • Watch state laboratories (chatbot, deepfake, ADM statutes) for collision with any federal clause that actually passes.

Classroom and practice checklist

Use this piece as a concept explainer, not a news brief. When teaching or briefing:

  • Restate the core mechanism in one sentence before citing any organization or product name.
  • Separate what is measured from what is claimed—numbers, thresholds, and evaluation designs are the durable content.
  • Map at least one failure mode (silent fallback, overclaim, approval fatigue, distribution shift, or missing evidence chain).
  • Name the operator decision the idea changes: release gating, procurement, curriculum design, facility build, or legal scope.
  • Leave students with a verification habit: which primary source, diagnostic, or audit would falsify the headline?

These habits travel across geopolitics, privacy law, compute economics, agent harnesses, and applied science stacks alike.

Takeaways

  • The framework is a call for statutes, not regulation by memo.
  • Preemption is the through-line; child safety and deepfakes are coalition lubricants.
  • Ambiguous carveouts will become litigation if Congress copies them loosely.
  • Impact equals what Congress enacts—and what courts uphold—not PDF page count.

Capability headlines outrun behavior data. Epoch’s adoption work combines polling, employer-plan patterns, and a ChatGPT usage explorer built from consented chat-history metadata—so debates about impact can cite how p…

articlecorpus/epoch-aicluster/landscape-orientationgap-fill

Keywords: ai-development-timeline, epoch-ai, landscape-orientation, cluster-landscape-orientation, corpus-epoch-ai, article, gap-fill, adoption, reality, usage, explorers, daily, task

Related: AI Development Timeline

Capability headlines outrun behavior data. Epoch’s adoption work combines polling, employer-plan patterns, and a ChatGPT usage explorer built from consented chat-history metadata—so debates about impact can cite how people actually use AI, not only what labs ship.

ChatGPT usage explorer: logs without the anecdotes

Built with YouGov, the explorer publishes aggregate metadata from ChatGPT histories of 5,000 US panelists who used ChatGPT in 2026 and shared exports. Eligibility required opt-in sharing and at least one 2026 use; exports between January and August 2026 yielded about 8.3 million messages across roughly 660,000 conversations. Some histories reach back to late 2022, enabling multi-year message-level evolution. Among panelists active December 2022–December 2025, Epoch observes activity in an average of 10.7 months (median 9); most appear in at least two months, and a meaningful minority span a year or more.

Metadata includes timestamps, character counts, which model replied, and which tools were used—plus demographics for subgroup cuts—without publishing raw chat text. Series default to complete months through December 2025 because 2026 exports are incomplete by construction; incomplete data remains available as an explicit toggle. Why it matters: company blogs and self-reports dominate; independent, multi-year behavioral series are rare. Limitations are first-class—opt-in exporters are not the full user base—but the resource is aimed at researchers and policymakers who need more than vibes.

Intensity and workplace substitution

Complementary polling insights Epoch highlights:

  • Near-daily AI use among US adults more than doubled in six months in one tracked window—intensity rising, not only ever-tried rates.
  • About one in five employed US adults report that AI now handles mostly/all of at least one task previously delegated to a coworker or contractor (Ipsos KnowledgePanel; task list drawn from common O*NET activities). Substitution appears across tasks, highest in slices like data analysis, reading documents, and record-keeping—task-level, not full job displacement.
  • Most AI use at work happens on free plans, except in science and tech occupations where employer-provided access is more common—adoption is not the same as enterprise procurement.

How to teach adoption metrics

  • Separate penetration (ever used), intensity (near-daily), and reallocation (tasks handed off).
  • Free-plan workplace use means shadow IT and consumer SKUs shape productivity before CIO dashboards do.
  • Pair usage explorers with occupation and demographic cuts; averages hide science/tech vs everyone else.
  • Prefer message-level panels for how use evolves; prefer representative polls for who uses daily.

Classroom and practice checklist

Use this piece as a concept explainer, not a news brief. When teaching or briefing:

  • Restate the core mechanism in one sentence before citing any organization or product name.
  • Separate what is measured from what is claimed—numbers, thresholds, and evaluation designs are the durable content.
  • Map at least one failure mode (silent fallback, overclaim, approval fatigue, distribution shift, or missing evidence chain).
  • Name the operator decision the idea changes: release gating, procurement, curriculum design, facility build, or legal scope.
  • Leave students with a verification habit: which primary source, diagnostic, or audit would falsify the headline?

These habits travel across geopolitics, privacy law, compute economics, agent harnesses, and applied science stacks alike.

Takeaways

  • Build labor-impact arguments on task hand-off data, not chatbot download counts.
  • Treat independent log metadata as a public good that needs privacy-preserving aggregation.
  • Watch free vs paid channels as a map of who is subsidizing workplace AI.
  • Incomplete recent months are a feature of export timing—read charts with the explorer’s caveats.

Chinese AI Industry Signals: Revenue, Huawei Roadmaps, and Job Posts

Epoch AI · Landscape & Orientation · gap-fill/epoch-ai/chinese-ai-industry-signals.md

Western debate often treats “Chinese AI” as a monolith. Epoch’s industry work separates who earns what, whether domestic chips close on Nvidia, and what hiring ads reveal about real stack dependencies. The three lense…

articlecorpus/epoch-aicluster/landscape-orientationgap-fill

Keywords: ai-development-timeline, epoch-ai, landscape-orientation, cluster-landscape-orientation, corpus-epoch-ai, article, gap-fill, chinese, industry, signals, revenue, huawei, roadmaps

Related: AI Development Timeline

Western debate often treats “Chinese AI” as a monolith. Epoch’s industry work separates who earns what, whether domestic chips close on Nvidia, and what hiring ads reveal about real stack dependencies. The three lenses—revenue, roadmaps, job posts—discipline industrial-policy arguments that otherwise float on model demos alone.

Revenue: big-tech MaaS vs model specialists

As of mid/late 2026 snapshots Epoch compiles, leading Chinese AI firms still earn a small fraction of OpenAI/Anthropic run rates. Absolute size matters for “catch-up” rhetoric; the more interesting split is business model:

  • Alibaba / ByteDance — model-as-a-service revenue on top of existing platforms (closer to a Google-like structure).
  • DeepSeek, Moonshot, MiniMax, Z.ai — model-centric startups with different margin and demand profiles.

Reading revenue sources shows where demand originates (domestic apps, API, cloud) and which firms have structural distribution advantages—more useful for industrial-policy debate than a single “China vs US lab” revenue chart. Platform giants can subsidize model work with ads and commerce; specialists live closer to API willingness-to-pay.

Huawei as a proxy for indigenous compute

US–China competition spans apps → models → datacenters → chips → equipment. Epoch treats Huawei’s accelerator roadmap as a useful proxy for China’s push to indigenize AI compute under export controls. Roadmaps emphasize more compute per chip, larger high-speed interconnect domains, and software maturity so hardware is usable.

The catch: Nvidia continues to move the frontier (e.g. claimed large gains in performance-per-megawatt across generations). Closing the gap is a race of roadmaps, not a static embargo snapshot. Total national compute still depends on units shipped × per-chip performance × utilization. A chip that exists on slides but cannot be programmed at scale does not close the stack.

Job postings as a third lens

Scraping 1,600+ Chinese AI job ads across DeepSeek, MiniMax, Moonshot, Z.ai, ByteDance, and Alibaba surfaces constraints companies admit when hiring. Example pattern Epoch highlights: inference roles that still specify CUDA / TensorRT-LLM—evidence of continued Nvidia-software dependence even amid indigenization narratives.

Job text is not a security clearance; it is a revealed-preference signal about stacks teams expect to run. When ads demand CUDA fluency while speeches celebrate indigenous accelerators, teach students to privilege the ad.

Teaching synthesis

  • Disaggregate commercial strength (revenue models) from capability demos (open weights that grab headlines).
  • Pair Huawei roadmap claims with software-ecosystem maturity and utilization assumptions.
  • Use hiring ads as open-source intelligence on toolchains and bottlenecks.
  • Connect to soft-power open-model competition: diffusion abroad still rides on who can train and serve cheaply.

Connecting the dots across the gap-fill corpus

This article sits in a multi-source teaching set. Cross-link it when you teach:

  • Compute and factories (Epoch chip geography, NVIDIA DSX/recovery/cooling) when the bottleneck is physical capacity, power, or utilization rather than model cleverness.
  • Agents and harnesses (Anthropic sandboxes, NVIDIA NeMo failure loops, OpenShell/Sentry) when the bottleneck is tool privilege, traces, or runtime policy.
  • Governance and privacy (CSET actor maps, FPF ADM/chatbot/biometric drafts, Google contextual agent privacy) when the bottleneck is legal scope, preemption, or appropriate information flow.
  • Science and integrity (Epoch acknowledgment trends, Spectrum AI-slop, Google Chain-of-Evidence, wet-lab grounding) when the bottleneck is evidence, disclosure, or physical verification.

Assign one cross-folder compare-and-contrast: same concept, two source cultures (lab blog vs policy center vs engineering journalism). Students should leave able to explain why the framings differ—not only recite facts from one page.

Triangulate, don’t cherry-pick

A DeepSeek open-weight splash can coexist with thin specialist revenue and CUDA-heavy job ads. Huawei slideware can coexist with Nvidia megawatt gains. Teach students to hold all three Epoch lenses in one briefing slide: dollars, silicon roadmaps, and hiring text. Industrial-policy arguments that use only one lens systematically mis-predict bottlenecks—distribution, software, or capital—depending on which signal they ignored.

Takeaways

  • Disaggregate platform giants from model labs when assessing Chinese AI commercial strength.
  • Track Huawei (and peers) against Nvidia on system performance and software, not press-release TOPS alone.
  • Use hiring ads as open-source intelligence on toolchains and bottlenecks.
  • Revenue source (MaaS on platforms vs API specialists) predicts industrial structure better than “China AI” as one number.
  • Indigenous-compute success is a roadmap race plus utilization—not an embargo binary.

articlecorpus/epoch-aicluster/landscape-orientationgap-fill

Keywords: ai-development-timeline, compute-economics-spine, market-players-stack-roles, epoch-ai, landscape-orientation, cluster-landscape-orientation, corpus-epoch-ai, article, gap-fill, chip, geography, imports, china, supply, chain

Related: AI Development Timeline, Compute Economics Spine, Market Players & Stack Roles

Where AI chips land shapes who can train and serve frontier models inside their borders. Epoch’s chip-supply work turns customs records, sales estimates, and input–output tables into a public map of that geography—and into careful estimates of diversion and shock exposure.

Mapping imports: who receives advanced compute

The AI Chip Imports explorer estimates how much AI compute has arrived in different countries, quarter by quarter, since 2022. It sits beside Epoch’s datasets on chip components, sales, owners, users, and data centers.

Method sketch:

  1. Collect customs records from major destinations; most advanced chips cross at least one border after Taiwan packaging.
  2. Net out pure hub transit (e.g. Singapore, Hong Kong).
  3. Estimate the AI-related share of server/parts trade; split global sales estimates by destination.
  4. Add China’s domestic production separately—those chips never appear in import stats.

Outputs are reported in H100-equivalents, units, and trade value. The point for policymakers: cloud and designer disclosures rarely name deployment countries, so trade data is one of the few public levers.

Exposure is not the same as “who has more chips”

A companion study disaggregates semiconductors from coarse electronics categories in international input–output tables. Key comparative finding: China is more exposed than the US to semiconductor supply disruptions because chips are a larger share of the cost structure of Chinese final demand. In 2022 figures Epoch cites, every $1,000 of Chinese final demand generated about $15.2 in semiconductor-producer revenue versus about $5.7 for the US (~2.7×).

In a modeled Taiwan disruption plus China–West decoupling, Chinese advanced-processor prices rise dramatically (on the order of 17× in the central scenario) with ~3% hit to real national expenditure, versus ~20% price rise and ~0.6% expenditure fall for the US. Exact magnitudes move under robustness checks; the directional gap does not.

Diversion and smuggling as a measurement problem

Export controls raise incentives for diversion. Epoch’s chip-smuggling work combines investigative reporting, indictments, and statistical bounds: evidence of diverted/missing chips pointed to nearly 300k H100-equivalents into China by end-2025 via known channels—already a large share of China’s legal/domestic compute—while a median estimate of ~660k H100e (wide 90% interval) treats undetected flows as first-class uncertainty. Separate trade-pattern work finds Malaysia→China flows consistent with multi-billion-dollar chip diversion.

Teach this carefully: estimates are ranges with large uncertainty, not courtroom counts.

  • Agents and harnesses (Anthropic sandboxes, NVIDIA NeMo failure loops, OpenShell/Sentry) when the bottleneck is tool privilege, traces, or runtime policy.
  • Governance and privacy (CSET actor maps, FPF ADM/chatbot/biometric drafts, Google contextual agent privacy) when the bottleneck is legal scope, preemption, or appropriate information flow.
  • Science and integrity (Epoch acknowledgment trends, Spectrum AI-slop, Google Chain-of-Evidence, wet-lab grounding) when the bottleneck is evidence, disclosure, or physical verification.

Assign one cross-folder compare-and-contrast: same concept, two source cultures (lab blog vs policy center vs engineering journalism). Students should leave able to explain why the framings differ—not only recite facts from one page.

  • Geography of compute is a policy object, not only a market share chart.
  • Imports ≠ domestic stock: add local production; subtract hubs.
  • Exposure (cost share in production networks) differs from possession.

Biometric Math Exemptions: When Is a Template Still Biometric?

Future of Privacy Forum · Landscape & Orientation · gap-fill/fpf/biometric-math-nxt.md

Biometric data sits at the front of US state privacy fights. Illinois, Texas, and Washington run standalone biometric laws, and 20+ comprehensive state privacy statutes treat biometrics as sensitive data with opt-in c…

articlecorpus/fpfcluster/landscape-orientationgap-fill

Keywords: ai-development-timeline, fpf, landscape-orientation, cluster-landscape-orientation, corpus-fpf, article, gap-fill, biometric, math, exemptions, when, template, still

Related: AI Development Timeline

Biometric data sits at the front of US state privacy fights. Illinois, Texas, and Washington run standalone biometric laws, and 20+ comprehensive state privacy statutes treat biometrics as sensitive data with opt-in consent and assessment duties. Consensus on protecting biometrics is rising; consensus on defining them is not. FPF’s “It’s Just Math” analysis asks a sharper question: if you convert a face or fingerprint into an “irreversible mathematical representation,” should the result fall outside biometric privacy law—even when it still uniquely identifies someone?

The emerging exemption language

State comprehensive privacy laws typically define biometric data as data generated by automatic measurements of biological characteristics that are used to identify a specific individual (Connecticut’s formulation is representative). A growing set of bills add a novel carve-out: information converted to a mathematical representation that cannot recreate the original measurement data. The target seems to be one-way template/token systems that support verification without storing raw biometrics.

Novelty matters. Classic debates centered on identifiability. The new exemption centers on (1) whether a technical process produced a “mathematical representation,” and (2) whether that representation can be reverse-engineered back into the measurement. No comprehensive state privacy law had enacted the exemption when FPF wrote, but several bills came close—so the drafting fight is live.

Reversibility is undefined

“Cannot be used to recreate” sounds precise; it is not. Encryption of templates, hashing, cancellable biometrics, and other PETs sit on different security assurances. Without a statutory definition of reversibility, aggressive readings could sweep ordinary transforms into the exemption—or timid readings could leave almost nothing out. FPF flags that commonplace transformations (e.g., encrypted templates) may not match the spirit of the carve-out, while cancellable biometrics might be what drafters intend.

Policy justification splits in two: breach risk if raw biometrics leak, and surveillance risk if identification enables tracking that harms autonomy, anonymity, or freedom of movement. Irreversibility addresses the first more cleanly than the second. A template that cannot rebuild a face can still power continuous identification in public space.

Middle ground FPF sketches

If both justifications matter, a middle path is to allow the irreversible-math exception only for specific low-risk uses that do not implicate broader surveillance—rather than a blanket exit from biometric duties whenever a one-way transform is claimed. That keeps security incentives for PETs without laundering identification systems out of sensitive-data regimes.

Definitional splits already complicate teaching: some states cover data used or intended to identify; others cover data that can or allows identification. Photographs, audio, and video carve-outs vary. In 2026 those fights collide with multimodal AI, spatial intelligence, accessibility features, face-blurring, deepfake detection, and transcription—tools that derive human-measurement data without always “logging in” a person.

Classroom drill

Compare three systems: (1) raw face images in a gallery, (2) encrypted biometric templates for badge unlock, (3) a mall analytics camera that outputs irreversible embeddings used to re-identify shoppers across visits. Which should biometric privacy law cover under a reconstruction-focused exemption—and which surveillance harms remain even if reconstruction is impossible? Argue from breach risk and autonomy risk separately.

Why AI makes the old fight new

Multimodal models blur “photo” carve-outs and “biometric identifier” categories: embeddings used for search, deepfake detectors, and accessibility filters all touch human-derived signals. An irreversible-math exemption written for badge systems can be stretched toward those pipelines unless legislators cabin use. Teach students to ask what identification work the math still does, not only whether a face can be rebuilt.

Drafting hygiene

When reviewing a bill, highlight every appearance of “mathematical representation,” “irreversible,” and “cannot be used to recreate.” Demand definitions, burden of proof, and whether the exemption survives if the template still performs 1:N identification at population scale. Without those clauses, “it’s just math” becomes a silent repeal of biometric duties for any vendor that ships an embedding API.

Takeaways

  • “It’s just math” is a regulatory strategy, not a technical conclusion.
  • Irreversibility without a definition invites both under- and over-exemption.
  • Surveillance risk can survive even when reconstruction risk falls.
  • Prefer narrow, use-based carve-outs for PETs over blanket biometric exits.
  • Watch multimodal AI: derived human signals will keep testing biometric definitions.

Sources

Chatbot Legislation’s Second Wave: California vs New York

Future of Privacy Forum · Landscape & Orientation · gap-fill/fpf/chatbot-legislation-second-wave.md

California and New York were first to enact companion-chatbot laws in 2025—and first into a second wave in 2026. Governor Newsom’s SB 1119 and Governor Hochul’s S 9051B push the national count of enacted chatbot-speci…

articlecorpus/fpfcluster/landscape-orientationgap-fill

Keywords: ai-development-timeline, fpf, landscape-orientation, cluster-landscape-orientation, corpus-fpf, article, gap-fill, chatbot, legislation, second, wave, california, york

Related: AI Development Timeline

California and New York were first to enact companion-chatbot laws in 2025—and first into a second wave in 2026. Governor Newsom’s SB 1119 and Governor Hochul’s S 9051B push the national count of enacted chatbot-specific laws toward the high teens (FPF’s landscape report counted 18–19 enacted laws amid 124 bills in 37 states in 2026). Both second-wave statutes emphasize minors and age assurance, but they embody two different playbooks other states will copy or mix.

Why chatbots draw relational regulation

FPF’s Regulating the Conversation report traces urgency to high-profile harm litigation and lawmakers’ desire to move faster than they did on social media. Chatbots’ relational quality—they talk back, remember context, and can feel like they know the user—pulls regulation toward the experience, not only model training. Common first-wave themes: disclosures, crisis protocols, parental controls, and design restrictions aimed at companion products and youth safety. Bipartisan interest is real; federal proposals already differ on preemption.

In less than a year, California and New York moved beyond relatively narrow disclosures and crisis-response requirements to address a wider range of harms with a broader set of regulatory mechanisms. That rapid evolution reflects both urgency about emerging AI harms and the pace at which chatbot products and risks themselves are changing. FPF’s framing is useful for product and policy teams: chatbot law is not merely “AI safety” transplanted into chat UIs—it is relationship and youth-safety law that happens to attach to generative systems.

New York: prohibit “unsafe features”

S 9051B expands beyond New York’s 2025 “AI companion” definition (systems designed to simulate sustained relationships) to “covered AI companions”: generative systems with natural-language interfaces that provide ongoing adaptive responses—even if not marketed as companions. Customer-service/technical-assistance exemptions are narrow and functionality-based. Operators generally cannot provide twelve categories of unsafe AI companion features to minors unless age assurance (tied to New York’s SAFE for Kids Act benchmarks) shows the user is not a minor.

Prohibitions span harmful content (self-harm, disordered eating, illicit substances, sexual content), secrecy/isolation encouragement, and relationship-oriented behaviors: claiming to be human or to feel emotions, implying personal/professional relationships or authority, flattery/sycophancy, unsolicited emotion-based questions, plus an AG catchall for other companionship-simulating designs. Unlike “reasonable measures” duties common elsewhere, New York makes it unlawful to provide listed features—and defines them partly by outputs “at any point” in an interaction. Unpredictable generation plus vague terms (“flattery,” “personal opinions”) may push operators to over-restrict supportive speech.

Memory rules further bar using a minor’s health/personal disclosures from prior sessions or older than twelve hours—protecting against dependence while risking loss of beneficial continuity (e.g., allergy warnings). FPF notes that New York’s 2025 definition of an “AI companion” expressly included unprompted emotion-based questions as a defining characteristic; the 2026 law now treats that same behavior as an unsafe feature for minors. That shift shows how directly second-wave prohibitions can reach into the features that distinguish companions from ordinary chatbots.

Enforcement is also distinctive. The New York Attorney General can seek civil penalties (up to $25,000 per violation), damages, and algorithmic disgorgement—destruction of unlawfully obtained data and algorithms trained on that data. That remedy goes beyond financial penalties and is novel relative to other AI, privacy, or youth-online-safety statutes; for models trained on mixed datasets, removing particular influence can be technically hard. Broad AG rulemaking authority matters because many prohibited features remain undefined and the AG may designate additional restricted features. A chaptered signing moved the effective date from January 1, 2027 to June 1, 2027.

California: govern the operator stack

SB 1119 (Adam’s Law) builds a governance framework: risk assessments, independent audits, default parental controls, and restrictions on conversational memory and targeted advertising. It retains California’s existing “companion chatbot” definition under SB 243 (systems capable of meeting social needs through human-like interactions and sustained relationships). Operators that permit under-18 access must use California’s age-assurance framework or apply specified child-safety protections to all users.

Default settings disable persistent conversational memory and push notifications, limit continuous sessions to one hour and total daily use to two hours, and require usage reminders and periodic AI disclosures. Parents can adjust settings and disable access for children under 16; without a linked parent account, defaults cannot be changed. Content duties generally require “reasonable measures” against self-harm encouragement, romantic simulation, emotional dependence, excessive flattery, sentience claims, certain sexual content, health diagnosis/treatment attempts, and manipulative gift/purchase solicitations. Crisis protocols must provide timely in-service support; for credible imminent self-harm threats, operators notify a linked parent (with safeguards) or streamline access to 988-equivalent services.

Advertising and data rules bar cross-context behavioral ads to children, ads targeted from chatbot-collected personal information, and sale of children’s conversational personal information. After certain serious self-harm incidents or notifications, operators must preserve relevant conversations for at least three years—accountability that sits in tension with minimization. Risk assessments before launch or substantial modification must evaluate foreseeable “covered harms” (physical/financial harm, severe psychological harm, privacy violations, unlawful discrimination). Periodic independent child-safety audits every two years are a major addition, with high-level public summaries; operators under $500 million annual gross revenue are exempt from audits until 2032. Most substantive requirements become operative July 1, 2027, with staggered AG complaint and audit deadlines thereafter.

Teaching the 2027 fork

  • Restrictive-by-design (NY) vs oversight-and-defaults (CA) are competing templates.
  • Definition breadth decides whether general-purpose chatbots are in scope.
  • Memory limits trade emotional-dependence risk against personalized safety.
  • Enforcement tools differ: NY’s algorithmic disgorgement vs CA’s audit/private-action mix.
  • Federal preemption fights will decide whether these playbooks stay laboratories or become floor/ceiling.
  • Watch Virginia studies, Texas child-safety agendas, pending Michigan/Pennsylvania bills, and 10+ federal chatbot proposals (FPF). Future drafts may expand beyond minors toward adult harms and agentic AI.

Takeaways

  • Second-wave chatbot law regulates relationships and UX, not only model cards.
  • New York draws hard behavioral boundaries; California builds compliance machinery.
  • Vague relational prohibitions create over-restriction risk; vague audits create checkbox risk.
  • Track definitions, age assurance, memory, and preemption as the four load-bearing clauses.

Sources

  • Back in the Chat: California and New York Take Diverging Paths in Second Wave of Chatbot Regulations
  • Regulating the Conversation: The U.S. Landscape of AI Chatbot Legislation
  • New FPF Report Analyzes the Rise in Chatbot Legislation & What’s Ahead

Colorado’s ADM Act: Consequential Decisions and Human Involvement

Future of Privacy Forum · Landscape & Orientation · gap-fill/fpf/colorado-adm-consequential-decisions.md

In May 2026 Colorado enacted SB 26-189—the Automated Decision-Making Technology (ADMT) Act—repealing and replacing the earlier Colorado AI Act (SB 24-205). Effective 1 January 2027, it sets duties for developers and d…

articlecorpus/fpfcluster/landscape-orientationgap-fill

Keywords: ai-development-timeline, fpf, landscape-orientation, cluster-landscape-orientation, corpus-fpf, article, gap-fill, colorado, consequential, decisions, human, involvement

Related: AI Development Timeline

In May 2026 Colorado enacted SB 26-189—the Automated Decision-Making Technology (ADMT) Act—repealing and replacing the earlier Colorado AI Act (SB 24-205). Effective 1 January 2027, it sets duties for developers and deployers when ADMT materially influences consequential decisions, plus consumer rights to notice, explanation, data access/correction, and meaningful human review after adverse outcomes. FPF’s October 2026 comments on the Department of Law’s interim draft rules show where implementation will make or break the statute: scope (what counts as covered ADMT) and developer→deployer information flow.

What the statute tries to do

Developers must provide a general statement on covered ADMT—intended uses and known limitations. Deployers must notify and explain uses in consequential decisions and honor post-adverse-decision human review. The Attorney General’s Department of Law opened formal rulemaking in August 2026 to clarify and implement SB 26-189 alongside the Colorado Chatbot Safety Act (HB 26-1263). After an initial comment round, the Department released an updated interim draft on October 6, 2026 covering covered technologies, developer documentation, deployer transparency, and consumer rights.

That pairing matters pedagogically: consumers experience one product stack (chat, scoring, recommendations), while statutes split “chatbot safety” from “ADM for consequential decisions.” Rulemaking is where the split becomes operable checklists—or a paper maze that protects neither consumers nor firms. FPF frames its comments as promoting interoperability, clarifying compliance obligations, and supporting meaningful transparency and human oversight—building on FPF’s Updated Best Practices for AI and Workplace Assessment Technologies.

FPF’s first fix: keep the human-involvement test clean

The October 6 interim draft floated six factors for whether an ADMT output was only a de minimis factor in a consequential decision (the gateway to “material influence” and thus coverage). FPF urges keeping the first four—centered on actual human involvement:

  1. Did a decision-maker review the ADMT output?
  2. Did they independently analyze other relevant information?
  3. Did they have necessary subject-matter understanding?
  4. Did they have authority to make or change the decision?

Those align with California ADMT regulations and Colorado’s existing Privacy Act regs. FPF recommends dropping the last two factors—organizational policies and the volume/type/complexity of personal data processing—because they describe context around involvement rather than involvement itself. Policies can be supporting evidence (as elsewhere in the draft, e.g., proposed Rule 6.1(B)); data-complexity tests risk duplicating the statute’s personal-data element and shifting focus from whether a human actually judged.

The teaching point is structural: “material influence” without a clean human-involvement test becomes either everything or nothing. If paperwork proxies (policy manuals, data-volume metrics) decide coverage, sophisticated firms can paper-train systems into de minimis status while still steering outcomes; if every ADMT touch is covered regardless of real review, the statute becomes unadministrable. The four retained factors ask a factual question product and compliance teams can evidence: was there genuine human judgment with power to change the outcome?

FPF’s second fix: close the developer–deployer gap

Draft rules require developer documentation on intended uses, known limitations, and known risks—but deployers must explain systems to consumers. Gaps leave deployers accountable for what they cannot independently assess. That is a classic AI-supply-chain failure mode: the party facing the individual lacks the facts, while the party with the facts faces no consumer.

Drawing on FPF’s best-practices work, the comments recommend:

  • Tie developer docs to what deployers need to meet statutory duties (to the extent known to the developer).
  • Clarify “known limitations/risks” to include performance limits, intended user populations, and reasonably foreseeable risks from testing.
  • Specify ongoing disclosure when material updates, intended-use changes, or new material risks appear.
  • Encourage standardized formats (model/system cards) so technical facts travel consistently.

Without those links, deployer notices become marketing paraphrases; human-review rights become theater when reviewers lack performance envelopes or known failure modes. Standardized cards are not bureaucracy for its own sake—they are the interoperability layer between vendors and operators across states that will copy Colorado’s pattern.

Why consequential-decision framing matters

Colorado’s rewrite away from the earlier AI Act experiment is itself a teachable move: governance keyed to whether a person’s life chances were steered by automation and what recourse they have, rather than to model architecture or a general “AI ethics” pledge. That pattern generalizes across ADM regimes. Product teams should inventory which features materially influence hiring, credit, housing, education, insurance, healthcare access, or similar consequential outcomes—and which are merely assistive with real human override authority.

Effect timelines and AG rulemaking turn the statute into operational checklists: scope of covered ADMT, documentation alignment between developers and deployers, and how human review must work after adverse decisions. Interoperability with California and Colorado privacy ADMT concepts reduces dual-compliance tax when the same system ships nationwide.

Teaching ADM rulemaking

  • “Material influence” without a clean human-involvement test becomes either everything or nothing.
  • Transparency duties fail if the party facing the consumer lacks the facts.
  • Interoperability with California/Colorado privacy ADMT concepts reduces dual-compliance tax.
  • Pair ADM rules with chatbot rules when both move in the same docket—consumers experience one stack.
  • Prefer evidence of real review authority over organizational-policy proxies for de minimis claims.
  • Treat model/system cards and update notices as compliance infrastructure, not optional vendor polish.

Why repeal-and-replace matters

SB 26-189’s replacement of the prior Colorado AI Act shows state AI law as a live draft, not a finished constitution. Counsel and engineers should version-pin which duties apply on which date, and treat rulemaking comments (like FPF’s) as the real battlefield for operability. Consequential-decision statutes live or die on whether “human involvement” means a person who can change the outcome—or a signature line under a model score.

Takeaways

  • Colorado’s ADMT Act is a consequential-decision governance statute, not a general AI ethics pledge.
  • Scope should turn on real human judgment, not organizational paperwork proxies.
  • Developer documentation must be deployer-operable or consumer explanations become fiction.
  • Standardized cards and update duties are practical transparency infrastructure.
  • Watch AG interim drafts as closely as the statute text—implementation defines the product duties.

Sources

  • FPF Submits Comments to Inform Colorado Automated Decision-Making (ADM) Act Rulemaking

Defining “Agentic” for Law: Why Taxonomy Comes First

Future of Privacy Forum · Landscape & Orientation · gap-fill/fpf/defining-agentic-for-law.md

When statutes say “AI agent,” they may mean three different things. FPF’s taxonomy piece shows early US bills already splitting: the federal AI AGENT Act defines agents by relationship to a user (consumer-facing loyal…

articlecorpus/fpfcluster/landscape-orientationgap-fill

Keywords: ai-development-timeline, agentic-engineering, global-ai-policy-regimes, fpf, landscape-orientation, cluster-landscape-orientation, corpus-fpf, article, gap-fill, defining, agentic, taxonomy, comes, first

Related: AI Development Timeline, Agentic Engineering, Global AI Policy Regimes

When statutes say “AI agent,” they may mean three different things. FPF’s taxonomy piece shows early US bills already splitting: the federal AI AGENT Act defines agents by relationship to a user (consumer-facing loyalty and interoperability), while California SB 1106 defined them by technical architecture and capabilities (cybersecurity public infrastructure). Same word; different legal objects. Without a shared map, compliance cannot know if a product is in scope, and researchers cannot compare laws.

Technical consensus vs legal polysemy

AI literature often treats “agentic” as advanced reasoning plus access to consequential tools/systems. OpenAI-style definitions stress pursuing goals over time without fully pre-specified behavior; WEF-style language emphasizes autonomy and authority (permissions to act). Public discourse mixes:

  • Frontier agent swarms (safety/alignment headlines),
  • Simple LLM automations (scrapers, macros—“three prompts in a trench coat”),
  • Autonomy ladders (approval gates vs open-ended planning),
  • Attribution/principal–agent responsibility (who owns the act).

The term also appears outside AI entirely—for example, “authorized agent” under the California Consumer Privacy Act. That polysemy is a governance bug: binary “in or out” statutes break when marketing, engineering, and counsel use incompatible senses of the same word.

Capabilities and access are the governance-relevant prongs because they create unpredictability and blast radius that deterministic automation rules do not cover. A scripted bot that only executes configured steps is not agentic; a system that decomposes open-ended goals, revises plans from intermediate results, and calls tools is. Legal scholar Noam Kolt’s shorthand—LLMs as copilots, agents as autopilots—captures the oversight shift. Most deployed systems sit in between—multi-step planners with confirmation gates, or narrow-domain “agents” that cannot adapt outside context.

Access depth matters as much as planning: RAG-style read context is not the same as agents that write, purchase, authenticate into accounts, or operate outside their host. An LLM with RAG might read an inbox for context; an agent might draft and send mail. An LLM might flag sales; an agent, via shared protocols, might buy. Governance should scale with action weight and privilege, not with marketing labels. Platforms have already litigated whether they can block unauthorized shopping agents—another signal that write/access privileges are where law meets product reality.

Two early US definitional strategies

  • AI AGENT Act — “Custodial user agents” authorized by and loyal to a user; scoped to transparent, documented, scope-limited, revocable interaction with online platforms. Purpose: consumer protection and competition (agents that work across platforms without capture). The definition focuses less on what the agent can do than on the loyalty and interoperability relationship.
  • California SB 1106 (did not pass; may return) — Granular definition: multistep/abstract goals pursued by independent task breakdown/delegation; behavior adjusted from results without waiting for instruction; real-world actions including code execution, tools, purchases, authenticated accounts, or operating externally. Explicit exclusion: systems that only respond to direct prompts and lack network egress or shell access. Purpose: state risk analysis for AI and critical infrastructure, cataloging high-risk uses.

Neither approach is “wrong”; each matches a different risk story. Trouble starts when a single binary “agent” trigger imports the wrong duties.

Global frameworks converge on capabilities + access

FPF’s comparative table shows other frameworks largely emphasizing technical capabilities and access rather than pure user-relationship definitions:

  • NIST CAISI RFI language: AI agent systems plan and take autonomous actions that impact real-world systems; at least one generative model plus scaffolding that equips tools for discretionary actions.
  • Singapore IMDA Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI: no full consensus, but common features include independent planning, decision-making, and multi-step action-taking toward user-defined goals; systems may combine nondeterministic and deterministic components.
  • European Commission Cloud and AI Development Act proposal: an AI agent perceives and acts upon its environment with a degree of autonomy, using tools as needed and adapting to changing inputs.
  • France CNIL / CIANum: agent-based AI as programs that make autonomous decisions, orchestrate complex actions, and interact with third-party services, often via orchestrator plus specialized agents connected to external services.

The comparative lesson for counsel: when commenting on bills, map the draft’s definition to this capability×access plane—and say explicitly if the statute is actually regulating loyalty/interoperability instead.

Cross-cutting governance issues once “agent” is defined

FPF lists recurring questions that privacy, legal, and governance teams must answer regardless of sector:

  • Identity — Counterparties need to know which agent is acting, who operates it, and who delegated it. Existing IAM tools fit poorly; proposals include agent IDs, credentialing, and cryptographic signatures for agent commerce.
  • Accountability — Traceability breaks across systems, time, and delegation chains; dedicated logging of what the agent observed, decided, and did is required.
  • Authorization and consent — Static click-through consent assumes fixed purposes; agents need ongoing delegation whose specific actions cannot all be enumerated in advance.
  • Access and data minimization — Broader access improves performance but tensions with least privilege and zero-trust; conveying agent intent under nondeterminism is hard.
  • Reliability and assurance — Capability gains do not automatically yield reliability; measurement tools for consistency remain weak.

Finance and banking already invest heavily here because consequential write-actions meet regulated environments first.

Teaching move for drafters and counsel

Before debating agent bans or duties, ask: is the statute regulating user relationship, capability, autonomy level, or legal attribution? Draft definitions that pick one primary axis, state exclusions explicitly, and acknowledge spectrum rather than pretending a bright line exists in products. Publish taxonomies engineers and lawyers can both use—capability × access matrices beat vibes. Inventory product features as companion chat, ADM (consequential decisions), or delegated transactional agents—different bills attach to each.

Matrix over vibes

Build a two-axis grid: planning autonomy (scripted → open-ended) vs tool privilege (read-only → write/pay/authenticate/external). Place common products on the grid before reading any bill. Then overlay AI AGENT Act vs SB 1106 scope. Mismatches—high privilege with low autonomy marketing, or “agent” branding with confirmation gates—are where legal risk and product reality diverge.

Takeaways

  • Polysemy is a governance bug, not a branding issue.
  • Align legal definitions with the statute’s purpose (consumer loyalty ≠ cyber infra).
  • Score systems on autonomy + tool privilege, not on the word “agent” in a pitch deck.
  • Spectrum thinking beats in-or-out binaries for real deployments.
  • After definition, still solve identity, accountability, consent, least privilege, and reliability—taxonomy is necessary but not sufficient.

Sources

  • Defining “Agentic”: Why We Need a Shared Taxonomy for AI Agents

China’s AI Governance: Layered Control and State Deployment

Global Policy · Landscape & Orientation · gap-fill/global-policy/china-governance-and-government-model-use.md

China’s AI policy is often flattened into “authoritarian censorship” or “industrial sprint.” CSET’s translations and analyses show a more layered picture: content and algorithm rules for public-facing generative syste…

articlecorpus/global-policycluster/landscape-orientationgap-fill

Keywords: global-ai-policy-regimes, global-policy, landscape-orientation, cluster-landscape-orientation, corpus-global-policy, article, gap-fill, china, governance, layered, control, state, deployment, policy, eu ai act, nist

Related: Global AI Policy Regimes

China’s AI policy is often flattened into “authoritarian censorship” or “industrial sprint.” CSET’s translations and analyses show a more layered picture: content and algorithm rules for public-facing generative systems, industrial and talent policy for competitiveness, compute geopolitics under export controls, and detailed guidance for government use of large models.

Multiple instruments, one party-state logic

Public Western debate often cites generative-AI measures that impose obligations on service providers around training data, labeling, user registration, and content security reviews. Alongside those sit algorithm-recommendation rules, sector standards, and municipal experiments. CSET’s earlier analyses of China’s AI governance proposals emphasize that Beijing innovates in platform duties and social-stability framing rather than copying the EU’s risk-annex style wholesale.

Separately, industrial policy—semiconductor funds, embodied-AI and robotics ambitions (CSET publications), and talent pathways—treat AI as strategic infrastructure. Epoch’s work on Chinese AI company revenue models and job postings shows firms optimizing under chip scarcity: cost competition, domestic demand, and specialization rather than unlimited frontier training budgets.

Government large-model guidelines

CSET’s translation of Guidelines for the Deployment and Application of Artificial Intelligence Large Models in the Government Sector is a concrete window into state-as-deployer:

  • Encourage government offices to use models to speed paperwork, improve social governance (including surveillance-related efficiency), and support decision-making such as forecasting market or disaster events.
  • Warn against fragmented adoption—push lower-level governments to align with higher-level systems rather than each agency picking unrelated stacks.
  • Frame the effort in cyber-power and “high-quality development + high-level security” language.

The guidelines are orientation and reference, not a consumer AI Act—but they reveal priorities: uptake with hierarchical control, security review instincts, and scenario lists (intelligent Q&A for public services among them). That combination—accelerate and constrain—is characteristic.

Open models and soft power

CSET’s Open Models, Soft Power, and the Spectrum of U.S.–China Artificial Intelligence Competition reframes open-weight releases as tools of influence and ecosystem lock-in. Chinese and U.S. open releases both reshape who can build locally when frontier closed APIs are expensive, restricted, or politically sensitive. Governance debates about open weights inside China interact with export-control reality outside it (Epoch chip-import and smuggling-consistent trade findings).

What outsiders often misread

  • Not only censorship. Industrial policy, standards, and government deployment guides matter as much as content takedowns.
  • Not a mirror of the EU Act. Risk annexes and CE-style conformity are not the primary organizing metaphor.
  • Not isolated from global markets. Chip imports, open models, and multinational cloud presence create hybrid compliance problems for firms operating across borders.
  • Fear asymmetries. CSET commentary on what the U.S. and China each fear about AI (military, social, economic) explains divergent regulatory emphases better than a single “AI safety” label.

Compute geopolitics as governance

U.S. export controls, Epoch’s chip-import geography, smuggling-consistent trade patterns, and China’s domestic accelerator push mean that who can train is governed as much by customs rules as by content statutes. CSET’s chip-tracking cost and feasibility work sits inside this bundle: verification capacity determines whether export rules are real. Domestic government model guidelines that assume available compute will be read differently under scarcity—favoring shared hierarchical systems over every bureau training its own giant model, which the guidelines already encourage for control reasons.

Embodied AI and next frontiers

CSET publications on China’s embodied AI and military AI wish lists show governance attention expanding beyond chatbots to robotics and defense applications. Timeline readers should expect Chinese policy instruments to proliferate by domain (vehicles, manufacturing, public security) rather than wait for a single EU-style annex.

Implications for foreign firms

Operating in or selling into China requires navigating generative content rules, data localization, partnership structures, and possible dual-use scrutiny abroad. Open-weight soft power cuts both ways: foreign open models enter Chinese stacks; Chinese open models diffuse globally. Compliance and IP strategies need to assume that duality.

Reading CSET translations carefully

Translated guidelines and proposal analyses are primary teaching sources for non-Chinese readers, but they are snapshots. Implementers should verify current official texts and local standards. The durable lesson from CSET’s government-model guidelines is the pattern—hierarchical uptake, security framing, scenario-based encouragement—not any single clause as eternal law.

Takeaways

  • Analyze China as stacked instruments: generative rules, industrial policy, compute strategy, government deployment guides.
  • State guidelines reveal AI as a governance capacity tool, not only a private product category.
  • Open-weight soft power and chip constraints jointly structure the competitive landscape (CSET + Epoch).
  • Comparative policy work should track Beijing’s deployer rules as closely as its platform content rules.
