Open AI Factory Platforms: Run:ai, DSX, and Predictable Capacity

NVIDIA Technical Blog · Inference, Efficiency & Infrastructure · gap-fill/nvidia-technical-blog/runai-dsx-open-platforms.md

AI factories turn energy into intelligence—but before the first token, operators must bring compute, networking, storage, power, cooling, and software online as one productive unit. Conventional builds serialize site…

articlecorpus/nvidia-technical-blogcluster/inference-infragap-fill

Keywords: llm-inference, nvidia-technical-blog, inference-infra, cluster-inference-infra, corpus-nvidia-technical-blog, article, gap-fill, open, factory, platforms, predictable, capacity

Related: LLM Inference

AI factories turn energy into intelligence—but before the first token, operators must bring compute, networking, storage, power, cooling, and software online as one productive unit. Conventional builds serialize site selection, power/cooling design, rack/cable install, network validation, and service bring-up; specialized labor and dependency delays push back the date infrastructure produces tokens. NVIDIA’s DSX AI Factory Platform story has two complementary teachables: open orchestration software (Run:ai) and modular, factory-built capacity (DSX POD), plus efficiency controls such as MaxLPS under power budgets.

Run:ai open source as DSX foundation

NVIDIA made the full Run:ai platform available as open source, establishing it as an open foundation inside DSX so ecosystem partners and AI clouds can raise workload throughput and GPU utilization on shared Kubernetes infrastructure. Run:ai has historically dynamically allocated GPU resources across data processing, training, and inference lifecycles. The open release includes the integrated platform plus independently adoptable components: KAI Scheduler, GPU Fractioning Operator, KAI Resource Management, and Workload Map (Karta), with additional platform code. Teams can adopt the whole, build products on top, or integrate individual components. Adoption paths include direct open-source install or DSX ecosystem partner offerings.

Teaching point: open orchestration is how factories avoid lock-in at the scheduling layer while still sharing operational patterns—fractional GPUs, fair-share, and lifecycle-aware placement—that determine realized utilization more than peak FLOPs marketing.

DSX POD: move integration upstream

DSX POD is a standardized, factory-built implementation model among DSX options. Partners build standardized containers that pre-integrate AI infrastructure, complete critical validation before shipment, and connect to prepared site infrastructure after delivery—reducing onsite integration complexity so operators reach productive capacity faster and more predictably. Rack-scale AI systems combine high-density compute, scale-up/scale-out networking, liquid cooling, power delivery, telemetry, and management software as one system; mechanical, electrical, thermal, and network requirements must stay in spec through factory integration, transport, install, and operation.

NVIDIA’s investment spans rack layout, structural loading, power, cooling, cabling, service access, reliability, and validation—extending the progression from chips/boards to rack-scale systems and SuperPOD-class reference architectures into a factory-built AI factory path. Containerization is not mandatory for every AI factory; conventional and onsite-integrated designs remain options. DSX POD adds a path where schedule predictability and reduced onsite work are priorities, aligned with platforms such as Vera Rubin in the reference design narrative.

Efficiency under power ceilings: MaxLPS

DSX MaxLPS addresses a different bottleneck: site power. Coordinated allocation adjusts participating GPU power limits so more productive work fits under the same managed power budget—validation and enforcement compare measured power against approved group budgets. An evaluation with Nscale on Blackwell Ultra (Kimi K2.5 FP4, Dynamo, TensorRT LLM, mixed high-throughput and low-latency instances) compared a static baseline (35 four-GPU nodes / 140 GPUs) to a MaxLPS configuration (48 nodes / 192 GPUs) that added another high-throughput instance while retaining low-latency capacity—measuring throughput, TTFT, latency, interactivity, and rack power so gains do not hide latency regressions. Teaching point: more GPUs under the same power envelope only help if software coordinates power and workload profiles.

How to teach open factory platforms

  • Separate orchestration openness (Run:ai/KAI) from physical bring-up models (POD vs onsite).
  • Measure time-to-first-productive-token and sustained utilization, not only install day photos.
  • Treat fractional GPU and scheduler policy as product features for multi-tenant factories.
  • Under constrained power, teach coordinated power limits as a first-class capacity lever.
  • Map which layer owns failures: scheduler vs node health vs workload recovery (see companion recovery article).

Takeaways

  • Open Run:ai + modular DSX POD + power-aware controls are the software/hardware bring-up story beyond chips.
  • Adopt Run:ai whole or as KAI/fractioning components—match integration depth to your platform team.
  • Factory-built PODs trade onsite work for schedule predictability; they do not obsolete all conventional builds.
  • MaxLPS-style coordination stretches productive work under fixed power budgets—measure latency alongside throughput.
  • Utilization is a systems property of schedulers, power, cooling, and recovery—not a GPU SKU alone.

Visual AI Agents: Cut Build Time and Runtime Tokens

NVIDIA Technical Blog · Inference, Efficiency & Infrastructure · gap-fill/nvidia-technical-blog/visual-ai-agents-cost-control.md

Visual AI agents that watch warehouses, factories, or cities fail economically in two places: composition time (weeks of microservice wiring) and runtime tokens (VLMs scoring every patch of every frame). NVIDIA VSS Bl…

articlecorpus/nvidia-technical-blogcluster/inference-infragap-fill

Keywords: llm-inference, nvidia-technical-blog, inference-infra, cluster-inference-infra, corpus-nvidia-technical-blog, article, gap-fill, visual, agents, build, time, runtime, tokens

Related: LLM Inference

Visual AI agents that watch warehouses, factories, or cities fail economically in two places: composition time (weeks of microservice wiring) and runtime tokens (VLMs scoring every patch of every frame). NVIDIA VSS Blueprint 3.3 attacks both: a Build Vision Agent skill that composes validated deployments from intent, and adaptive EVS (Efficient Video Sampling) that prunes unchanged visual tokens and batches VLM work around moments when something happens.

Development cost: compose, don’t rebuild

Earlier VSS skills handled individual operations—deployment, camera setup, summarization, search, alerts, analytics. VSS 3.3 organizes them as deployment skills, operation skills, tools, and benchmarks, with vss-build-vision-ai composing the rest. Developers describe the application they want; the Build Vision Agent skill translates intent into a deployment plan spanning profiles, microservices, configuration, and runtime operations. Rather than generating a stack from scratch, the skill starts from the closest of four validated developer profiles, then extends a running deployment without rebuilding the whole stack—traffic management and incremental change included.

The teaching metaphor in the blog animation: one prompt becomes a composed, validated, running visual AI agent (e.g., warehouse) that returns confirmed/rejected search clips and a reasoned answer to questions like “Is this a safety violation?” Composition blueprints and coding-agent skills that emit deploy plans cut build time the way EVS cuts runtime.

The four Foundation profiles are concrete capability stacks, not vague templates: base (VLM dense captioning and Q&A on clips), alerts (real-time VLM alerting, or RT-CV detection with behavior analytics and VLM alert verification), lvs (long video summarization), and search (object/video embeddings with agentic search). The skill picks the closest Foundation by delta size, then adds or removes only exact service keys, keeps services a requested capability actually reaches, and converges shared roles onto one instance—two capabilities that need a detector share one detector; Kafka/Elasticsearch are shared with separate indices. When rules cannot settle a choice, the skill asks one structured question instead of guessing. That delta discipline is the anti-pattern to “generate a whole Compose file from a vibe.”

Runtime cost: adaptive EVS

EVS already ships in vLLM and Cosmos NIM microservices at a fixed pruning rate. The adaptive version in VSS 3.3 integrates into the real-time VLM microservice and decides which tokens to keep per patch and per frame, pruning parts of a frame that did not change versus the previous one and batching VLM work around change events. Static scenes flatten EVS gains; realistic change rates and concurrent streams per GPU are the right benchmarks.

Separate composition time from runtime tokens in TCO models. A team can win on build time with the Build Vision Agent skill and still lose in production if every camera stream pays full VLM tokens on empty corridors. Conversely, aggressive pruning without recall SLOs on held-out incident clips creates silent safety debt. Keep detection→retrieval→summary as a pipeline with evals at each stage so cheaper sampling does not silently drop safety-critical frames. Extend running deployments rather than rebuilding—traffic management and incremental capability adds are first-class in the 3.3 skill model.

Why visual agents are different from chat agents

Chat agents mostly pay for text tokens; visual agents pay for pixels × streams × time. That changes architecture: you need shared infrastructure (message buses, indexes, detectors) amortized across capabilities, and you need sampling policies that track scene dynamics. Teaching should therefore include both a composition lab (start from search vs alerts Foundations and measure delta size) and a runtime lab (fixed EVS vs adaptive EVS under scripted motion). Pair with edge bring-up when cameras sit far from the data center—token economics and device constraints interact.

Teaching visual-agent economics

  • Instrument tokens/frame, GPU-seconds/stream, and false-negative rate on held-out incident clips together.
  • Prefer extending validated profiles over greenfield YAML archaeology.
  • Treat adaptive sampling as a product feature with safety SLOs—not only a cost knob.
  • Benchmark concurrent streams under realistic motion; idle corridors overstate savings.
  • Pair with edge bring-up literacy when cameras sit far from the data center.

Takeaways

  • Visual agents are systems-cost problems, not only model-quality problems.
  • Invest in composition blueprints and adaptive sampling.
  • Raw VLM quality without token economics will not survive multi-stream production.
  • Coding-agent skills that emit deploy plans cut build time the way EVS cuts runtime.
  • Measure safety recall alongside $/stream—cost wins that miss incidents are not wins.

Related: Generative AI Cost Operating Model, Model Routing

Frontier labs now ship families of models (max-intelligence, strong mid-tier, fast/cheap) plus knobs for reasoning effort and speed. Treating “one model for everything” as a moral stance is how teams burn 10–100× too much money—or ship brittle agents on the wrong tier.

Match capability to the job

A practical routing map:

TierUse when
Max frontier (e.g. Astra-class)Hardest reasoning, novel debugging, long-horizon agent coordination, optimizing other systems
Strong efficient (e.g. Sol / Terra-class)Complex coding, document work, computer use at production volume
Focused / high-QPS (e.g. Luna-class, Decisions)Classification, extraction, routing, structured micro-decisions

Within a model, reasoning effort (low → max) and speed modes (standard / fast / ultrafast) are separate axes: more thought ≠ always better; ultrafast helps interactive loops even when reasoning stays moderate.

Production efficiency levers

Before you “need a smarter model,” check:

  • Prompt caching — put stable instructions and tools first; volatile task data last. Cached input can cost ~95% less.
  • Compaction — shrink long-running context while preserving state.
  • Parallel independent work — don’t serialize unrelated tool waits.
  • Cost per successful task — not cost per token alone; failed cheap runs are expensive.

Case study pattern: cache policy beats model shopping alone

Asana’s browser-agent study is instructive. An engineer used a top-tier model to investigate the agent: it cached fixed instructions but not growing page history, and trimmed screenshots every step—destroying cache continuity. After controlled experiments on history budgets and screenshot batching, the optimized workflow on an efficient frontier model ran about 76× cheaper and 5× faster than the original production setup. Separately, LegalOn-style orgs cut Codex spend ~50% by guidelines that map task complexity and growth stage to model choice—without freezing development velocity.

Long-running control plane

For hour/day-scale work: mid-turn steering, async tools, subagent delegation, and explicit “ask vs proceed” boundaries matter as much as which weights you call. Computer use belongs only where APIs cannot; prefer the simplest reliable tool for each step.

Rule of thumb: use the most capable model to design and optimize the harness; use the cheapest model that hits your eval bar to run it at scale.

Energy, Goodput, and the Physics of Frontier AI

Sequoia · Inference, Efficiency & Infrastructure · sequoia/energy-and-goodput.md

Model-quality narratives often ignore the industrial reality underneath: frontier AI is becoming an energy-and-systems problem as much as an algorithms problem. Sequoia conversations with Crusoe’s Chase Lochmiller, Google’s Amin Vahdat, NVIDIA’s Jensen Huang, and Starcloud’s…

articlecorpus/sequoia-ai-knowledgecluster/inference-infra

Keywords: memory-wall, energy-goodput-constraints, sequoia, inference-infra, cluster-inference-infra, corpus-sequoia-ai-knowledge, article, energy, physics, goodput

Related: Energy & Goodput Constraints, Memory Wall

Model-quality narratives often ignore the industrial reality underneath: frontier AI is becoming an energy-and-systems problem as much as an algorithms problem. Sequoia conversations with Crusoe’s Chase Lochmiller, Google’s Amin Vahdat, NVIDIA’s Jensen Huang, and Starcloud’s Philip Johnston push the same lesson from different altitudes—electrons, failure physics, paid useful work, and even whether Earth remains the cheapest place to put compute.

Definition: feedstock, factories, and goodput

Treat three terms as load-bearing.

AI factory. Huang’s framing: not a metaphor for “a big GPU pile,” but an industrial stack that turns power and capital into generated intelligence—chips and networking, land/power/shell/ops, models, and finally agentic systems that do paid work. The layers below the model (power, packaging, fabrics, cooling) are no longer background; they are the scarce inputs.

Stranded (or underpriced) energy → intelligence. Lochmiller’s Crusoe thesis, signaled in Sequoia’s “turning stranded energy into intelligence” framing, is geographic and thermodynamic: site compute where electrons are abundant or underutilized, and treat power as the feedstock of training and inference. Even without a complete transcript of that interview in the local corpus, the strategic claim is the one builders keep rediscovering—site selection is model strategy.

Goodput. Vahdat’s corrective to vanity metrics: not peak FLOPS on a slide, but the useful work a workload actually delivers after slowdowns, failures, restarts, and recovery. Throughput says you are busy; goodput asks whether you finished the job you cared about, on the wall-clock that finance feels.

Mechanism: why physics shows up in the P&L

At small scale, a failed accelerator is an annoyance. At 1,000–100,000 tightly synchronized accelerators—Vahdat’s concrete range—components must coordinate at microsecond-to-millisecond granularity. One stop can stall the synchronous job. Then you ask: which unit failed, what checkpoint exists, how do we restore, or must we restart from the beginning? He notes that at ~100,000-accelerator scale, something fails multiple times an hour. Detection, telemetry, and near-real-time recovery become first-class systems work; optical tricks (e.g., rerouting light to a spare rack in milliseconds) exist because waiting on human ops is too slow.

That is why “buy more GPUs” is an incomplete scaling plan. Networking, checkpoint discipline, storage bandwidth, and CPU/host capacity matter—especially as long-horizon agents drive demand for CPUs and storage alongside accelerators. The economics follow: theoretical teraflops that die in recovery tax are not what you bought.

Huang’s commercial mechanism closes the loop. Early generative systems could impress without being valuable in the labor sense. Once systems become agentic—able to use tools and produce useful work—you can pay for them by the hour (he cites everyday paid usage on the order of tens of dollars per hour of work). Monetized useful work justifies infrastructure spend; it also intensifies competition for every scarce layer of the cake: silicon, networking, land, power, and operators.

Starcloud pushes the boundary further. Johnston argues declining launch costs plus rising terrestrial energy and land constraints could make space-based data centers competitive: continuous high-intensity solar without atmosphere, and a cost curve that may fall while Earth sites get harder. The hard problems, in his telling, are heat and radiation—vacuum makes heat rejection difficult despite the “space is cold” intuition—not a sci-fi cold-room fantasy. Whether or not you buy the timeline, the teaching point stands: long-run compute location is a physics-and-capex question, not only a cloud SKU question.

Practice implications for builders

  • Price reliability into TCO. GPU list price ignores restart tax, idle during recovery, and engineer time spent on failed runs.
  • Instrument goodput. Track delivered useful work for your training and serving jobs under real failure conditions—not brochure FLOPS.
  • Design for partial failure. Checkpoint cadence, restart granularity, and fabric redundancy are product features of the training system.
  • Site for power and latency. Energy availability, interconnection queues, cooling water/air, and distance to users are roadmap inputs.
  • Expect agentic load shapes. Agents stretch host CPU, storage, and network differently than pure dense matmuls; capacity plan accordingly.
  • Treat energy timing as near-term. Constraint arrival is measured in years of interconnection and generation buildout—not abstract decades.

Failure modes

  • FLOPS vanity. Celebrating cluster size while goodput collapses under correlated failures.
  • Synchronous fragility. Architectures that assume perfect uptime at 100k-scale coordination.
  • Power-last planning. Choosing regions for talent branding while interconnection queues make GPUs orphaned assets.
  • Ignoring the stack below the model. Underinvesting in networking, checkpoint storage, and ops telemetry.
  • Paying for intelligence, not work. Deploying chat novelty without a path to billable useful work that funds the factory (Huang’s value distinction).
  • Earth-only dogma—or space hype without thermal math. Either dismissing location physics or hand-waving heat/radiation.

Practice checklist

  • Budget reliability, checkpoint, and restart cost into training TCO—not only accelerator sticker price
  • Track goodput and utilization beside model quality metrics on every major run
  • Make site selection an explicit AI strategy decision: power, cooling, latency, and expansion headroom
  • Capacity-plan CPUs, storage, and network for agentic workloads, not only dense training
  • Prefer designs that degrade and recover locally over all-or-nothing synchronous failure
  • Assume energy and interconnection constraints arrive on business-planning horizons, not “someday”
  • Revisit whether incremental demand should buy more chips, more reliability software, or a different site

Intelligence Per Watt: Rethinking the Computing Substrate

Sequoia · Inference, Efficiency & Infrastructure · sequoia/substrate-intelligence.md

Most AI efficiency work optimizes algorithms or GPU kernels. Naveen Rao (Unconventional AI) argues the deeper limit is the physical substrate of computation—and that brains are an existence proof the industry underweights. The teaching frame is intelligence per watt: useful…

articlecorpus/sequoia-ai-knowledgecluster/inference-infra

Keywords: energy-goodput-constraints, ai-designed-chips, sequoia, inference-infra, cluster-inference-infra, corpus-sequoia-ai-knowledge, article, substrate, per, computing

Related: AI-Designed Chips, Energy & Goodput Constraints

Most AI efficiency work optimizes algorithms or GPU kernels. Naveen Rao (Unconventional AI) argues the deeper limit is the physical substrate of computation—and that brains are an existence proof the industry underweights. The teaching frame is intelligence per watt: useful cognition delivered per unit energy, not FLOPS marketed on a slide. Digital accelerators improved cost and packaging faster than true energy per useful operation once memory traffic is counted. If AGI-scale ambition collides with the grid, substrate becomes strategy.

The energy wall

Human brains run on roughly 20W each. Aggregate that across humanity and you get on the order of ~160GW of biological compute—set against global electrical capacity measured in thousands of gigawatts, with AI training and inference racing to claim an alarming share. Rao’s point is not a precise forecast of blackouts; it is that energy, not ideas, becomes the binding constraint within a few years if trajectories continue.

Biology’s gap versus machines is not a rounding error. A macaque brain is probably under a watt; complex mammalian and insect behaviors run on milliwatts. A phone is about a watt; a squirrel leaping branch to branch may run on less than 10mW—on the order of 1/100 of that phone—while solving perception and control problems we still struggle to match with much larger computers. Tokens-per-second favor machines; discovery-grade intelligence still looks expensive in joules.

Thermodynamic and lithographic bounds

There is a physical asymptote: the Landauer principle bounds how much irreversible computation you can buy per unit energy. Biology sits high on the efficiency curve after billions of years of evolution, yet Rao places it still perhaps ~100× (an order or two of magnitude) short of that thermodynamic limit. Modern digital practice sits far lower. Limits of 2D lithography define another ceiling for conventional chips. Focused effort might push toward lithography’s edge—still, in his sketch, something like three orders of magnitude better than where we are today on energy efficiency—and still short of biology’s neighborhood, let alone Landauer.

Crucially, advertised FP8 flop efficiency has not moved like sticker prices: manufacturing and packaging got cheaper; energy per flop with memory access improved only incrementally. That is why “buy more GPUs” is a cost story that eventually becomes a physics story.

Mechanism: non-von Neumann dynamics

Brains do not primarily compute by matrix math on a von Neumann shuttle between memory and ALU. They use nonlinear dynamics: time-varying interactions among neurons are the compute. The systems are stochastic; they are not brittle one-and-zero machines where a single bit flip voids the program.

Rao’s engineering direction: trainable coupled oscillators and related dynamical circuits. Classic Kuramoto synchronization shows rigidly coupled oscillators converging regardless of start state. Generalize to a trainable coupling fabric and the system can traverse rich state-space trajectories. Training becomes steering those trajectories—not endlessly writing tensors out, operating, and writing back. In his demo framing, physics runs after an initial condition (and optional early error signal); state is implicit in the evolving system. Energy burns less on memory traffic because state and function overlap.

This is truly non-von Neumann relative to CPUs (fast single-thread memory loops), GPUs (wide operand batches still crossing memory), and even compute-in-memory designs that still largely linearize time. Unconventional’s claim is not that GPUs stop mattering tomorrow, but that ASI-level abundance likely needs a different abstraction than 1940s digital floating-point machines adapted to other workloads.

Startup advantage, in his telling, is lack of baggage: months from no team to prototype tapeout cycles versus incumbent roadmaps—accelerated by using AI in the design loop itself.

Why builders should care now

Even if you never fabricate oscillators:

  • Make energy per task a first-class KPI alongside latency and quality.
  • Expect co-design between models and machines to intensify; architectures that assume infinite HBM movement will age poorly.
  • Plan products and margins for a world where “just scale the cluster” collides with power delivery, not only chip supply.
  • Watch substrate research as option value: the winners of the next decade may own different primitives than CUDA comfort suggests.

Failure modes

  • Confusing cheaper tokens with thermodynamic progress.
  • Ignoring memory movement when quoting efficiency.
  • Betting entire roadmaps on unbounded digital scale without power, cooling, and siting plans.
  • Dismissing biology as metaphor only—then being surprised when efficiency gaps dominate unit economics.
  • Overclaiming near-term replacement of GPUs; the honest stance is parallel research, not instant substitution.

Practice checklist

  • Report joules (or watts × time) per successful task in internal dashboards
  • Separate algorithmic wins from packaging/cost wins in efficiency reviews
  • Include power and interconnect constraints in capacity planning, not only GPU counts
  • Prefer model/serving designs that reduce memory traffic for the same quality
  • Track substrate and unconventional-compute research as strategic awareness, not only vendor roadmaps
  • Avoid demo metrics that hide energy (e.g., quality at unlimited batching power)
  • When evaluating infra vendors, ask about energy per useful operation with memory, not peak FLOPS alone

Sources

  • Why the Brain Computes 1,000,000x More Efficiently Than A GPU: Unconventional AI's Naveen Rao

Voice AI Latency Budgets: Sub-100ms Speech and Measured Autoscaling

AWS ML Blog · Physical AI, Voice & Autonomy · extra/aws-ml-blog/voice-ai-latency-budget.md

Natural conversation has a temporal window. If synthesized speech arrives outside human turn-taking expectations, users hear awkward pauses, trust drops, and contact-center or sales agents lose the floor. Voice AI is

articlecorpus/aws-ml-blogcluster/physical-ai

Keywords: voice-as-primary-interface, generative-ai-cost-operating-model, aws-ml-blog, physical-ai, cluster-physical-ai, corpus-aws-ml-blog, article, latency, tts, speech

Related: Generative AI Cost Operating Model, Voice as Primary Interface

Natural conversation has a temporal window. If synthesized speech arrives outside human turn-taking expectations, users hear awkward pauses, trust drops, and contact-center or sales agents lose the floor. Voice AI is therefore an infrastructure latency problem as much as a model-quality problem.

Why transformers struggle at the edge of perception

Many TTS stacks wait for a full text sequence before audio. Quality and latency trade off. Architectures that process audio as evolving state—state space models (SSMs) with fixed-size hidden state and token-by-token recurrence—are a better fit for streaming speech: constant memory, native streaming, long-range dependencies without quadratic attention cost. Production systems report ~90ms time-to-first-audio-byte as a realistic “feels human” target for TTS, with STT that emits partial transcripts and semantic end-of-turn detection so the LLM can start thinking before the user fully stops speaking.

Close the “wait for the whole answer” gap

Even with a fast TTS model, a common agent bug remains: the LLM generates a multi-paragraph reply, and TTS only starts after the full string arrives. Users hear silence for seconds while the answer already exists in partial form.

Fix: stream sentence by sentence (or similar phrase boundaries) from the agent to TTS as soon as each unit is complete. Host a small TTS model on a real-time GPU endpoint if you need cost control; expose both unary streaming and bidirectional WebSocket-style routes when the transport requires it. First audio can start while later sentences are still being generated.

Stop guessing autoscaling targets

TTS endpoints fail silently when scale targets are vibes:

  • Too conservative → GPUs idle on every invoice.
  • Too aggressive → concurrency exceeds what one instance can serve inside the SLO; queues explode exactly when call volume peaks.

Replace guesses with two measurements on the live endpoint:

  • Q_max — highest concurrency one instance sustains before breaching the latency SLO.
  • T_total — end-to-end scale-out time (including cold start).

Derive scale-out threshold, scale-in threshold, and cooldowns from those numbers by arithmetic. Re-measure when model, instance type, or SLO changes.

Deployment constraints

Contact centers, telehealth, and regulated workloads often need inference in-VPC with data residency. Marketplace/SageMaker-style private endpoints and careful regional placement matter as much as model choice. Pair low-latency synthesis with accurate reading of numbers, currency, and addresses when the voice stack is order-confirmation critical.

Takeaway

Budget latency like an SLO: architecture for streaming (SSM or equivalent), sentence-level handoff from LLM to TTS, and autoscaling constants measured from Q_max and T_total—not dashboard defaults.

China’s Embodied AI: A Different Path Toward AGI

CSET Georgetown · Physical AI, Voice & Autonomy · gap-fill/cset-georgetown/chinas-embodied-ai-path.md

Western AGI debates often equate progress with scaling LLMs. CSET’s December 2025 report *China’s Embodied AI: A Path to AGI* (Hannas, Chang, Weber, Chou) documents a broader Chinese research and industrial bet: intel…

articlecorpus/cset-georgetowncluster/physical-aigap-fill

Keywords: physical-ai-robotics, cset-georgetown, physical-ai, cluster-physical-ai, corpus-cset-georgetown, article, gap-fill, china, embodied, different, path, toward

Related: Physical AI / Robotics

Western AGI debates often equate progress with scaling LLMs. CSET’s December 2025 report China’s Embodied AI: A Path to AGI (Hannas, Chang, Weber, Chou) documents a broader Chinese research and industrial bet: intelligence that emerges from body–brain–environment interaction—robots, drones, vehicles, and simulated worlds—not only from next-token prediction. The point is not that China ignores large models; it is that embodiment is treated as a parallel path to AGI and a commercial industrial strategy at once.

Two theories of the path

In the US and Europe, many labs still treat LLMs and multimodal variants as the most promising AGI route despite known limits in abstraction, grounding, and reliable reasoning. Chinese discourse—backed by national and local policy—more often treats human-level intelligence as inseparable from acting under physical constraints. LLMs learn heavily from depictions of the world; embodied systems learn from closed-loop interaction with it (and with high-fidelity simulation).

CSET’s executive framing: China aims to accomplish two goals simultaneously—enriching the real economy by integrating AI into physical production and services, and pursuing AGI “more aligned with the totality of human expression.” Coastal provinces and cities have stood up large embodied AI innovation centers linked to top universities and tech firms. That infrastructure map—who funds centers, which firms co-locate, which academic programs reorient—is a leading indicator alongside model release blogs.

Competition literacy without hype

Embodied AI reframes what “winning” looks like:

  • Metrics shift from chat/coding leaderboards toward manipulation, navigation, sim-to-real transfer, and closed-loop control reliability.
  • Manufacturing strength becomes an AI input: factories, component supply, and robotics OEMs are part of the stack, not a separate industrial story.
  • Dual-use adjacency is real—civilian automation sits next to autonomous systems—but teaching should stick to documented programs and RFP patterns rather than speculative weapons laundry lists.
  • Allied policy takeaway in the report: ramp up monitoring and claim benchmarking, and consider AGI approaches beyond “scale the next LLM.”

For students of geopolitics, DeepSeek-class open weights and embodied robotics are not competing narratives; they are different instruments in a portfolio strategy.

How to read Chinese embodiment claims

  • Prefer center openings, funding notices, and academic curricula over marketing demos.
  • Separate simulation progress from real-world robustness; sim-ready is not deploy-ready.
  • Ask what bottleneck binds: data of physical interaction, actuators, energy, or model brains?
  • Pair with PLA C5ISRT demand signals and civil chip/workforce policy for a full picture of physical AI ambition.

Connecting the dots across the gap-fill corpus

This article sits in a multi-source teaching set. Cross-link it when you teach:

  • Compute and factories (Epoch chip geography, NVIDIA DSX/recovery/cooling) when the bottleneck is physical capacity, power, or utilization rather than model cleverness.
  • Agents and harnesses (Anthropic sandboxes, NVIDIA NeMo failure loops, OpenShell/Sentry) when the bottleneck is tool privilege, traces, or runtime policy.
  • Governance and privacy (CSET actor maps, FPF ADM/chatbot/biometric drafts, Google contextual agent privacy) when the bottleneck is legal scope, preemption, or appropriate information flow.
  • Science and integrity (Epoch acknowledgment trends, Spectrum AI-slop, Google Chain-of-Evidence, wet-lab grounding) when the bottleneck is evidence, disclosure, or physical verification.

Assign one cross-folder compare-and-contrast: same concept, two source cultures (lab blog vs policy center vs engineering journalism). Students should leave able to explain why the framings differ—not only recite facts from one page.

Classroom and practice checklist

Use this piece as a concept explainer, not a news brief. When teaching or briefing:

  • Restate the core mechanism in one sentence before citing any organization or product name.
  • Separate what is measured from what is claimed—numbers, thresholds, and evaluation designs are the durable content.
  • Map at least one failure mode (silent fallback, overclaim, approval fatigue, distribution shift, or missing evidence chain).
  • Name the operator decision the idea changes: release gating, procurement, curriculum design, facility build, or legal scope.
  • Leave students with a verification habit: which primary source, diagnostic, or audit would falsify the headline?

These habits travel across geopolitics, privacy law, compute economics, agent harnesses, and applied science stacks alike.

Takeaways

  • Do not read Chinese AGI strategy as “just DeepSeek.”
  • Embodiment is simultaneously industrial policy and a theory of intelligence.
  • Watch regional innovation centers and university–firm loops as leading indicators.
  • Benchmark embodied claims with the same skepticism applied to LLM demos—and with different metrics.

Gemini Robotics: Whole-Body Physical AI

DeepMind Blog · Physical AI, Voice & Autonomy · extra/deepmind-blog/gemini-robotics-physical-ai.md

Physical AI needs more than a chatbot that describes actions. Gemini Robotics 2 splits the stack into complementary models so robots can reason for minutes, control whole bodies, and run locally when the network is

articlecorpus/deepmind-blogcluster/physical-ai

Keywords: world-models, physical-ai---robotics, deepmind-blog, physical-ai, cluster-physical-ai, corpus-deepmind-blog, article, robotics, gemini, whole-body

Related: Physical AI - Robotics, World Models

Physical AI needs more than a chatbot that describes actions. Gemini Robotics 2 splits the stack into complementary models so robots can reason for minutes, control whole bodies, and run locally when the network is unavailable.

Three roles in one stack

| Model | Role | Job | | --- | --- | --- | | Gemini Robotics 2 (VLA) | Vision–language–action | Map vision + language to motor control for humanoids and bi-arm robots; finer dexterity on hands and grippers. | | Gemini Robotics ER 2 | Embodied reasoning agent | Talk with humans, understand the scene, plan multi-step tasks lasting several minutes, coordinate the VLA, track progress, collaborate across robots. | | Gemini Robotics On-Device 2 | Efficient local VLA | Run without cloud latency; adapt to new embodiments in a few hours (often under 200 examples) via motion-transfer techniques. |

This separation mirrors software agents: a planner/agent layer plus an executor, with an edge option when connectivity or latency constraints bite.

From tabletop to whole-body

Earlier systems focused on upper-body tabletop work. Whole-body control matters because human environments demand walking, crouching, balancing, and reaching in clutter. Examples include humanoids fetching and shelving objects, five-fingered hands tying knots or sealing bags, and gripper platforms packing tightly.

Agentic robotics behaviors

ER 2 is positioned as the high-level brain: decompose instructions, self-correct when a step fails, know when tasks start/end, and detect key events. Multi-robot collaboration lets heterogeneous robots share a workflow one body could not finish alone.

Safety advances include ASIMOV-Agentic-style benchmarks for refusing unsafe tool calls from the VLA, predicting task feasibility, and requesting human help under uncertainty—plus proximity-aware stops when people approach.

Embodiment transfer

A persistent robotics bottleneck is that skills learned on one body rarely transfer. On-Device 2’s few-hour adaptation across platforms with different shapes, sensors, and degrees of freedom is the teachable claim: treat embodiment shift as a data-efficient adaptation problem on a general VLA prior, not a full retrain per robot.

Lessons for physical AI builders

  1. Separate reasoning agent from motor policy; keep a human-communication channel on the agent.
  2. Optimize an on-device path early if latency or offline operation matters.
  3. Evaluate long-horizon progress tracking and multi-robot protocols, not only single grasps.
  4. Add agentic safety tests (refuse unsafe acts, ask when uncertain) alongside classical collision safety.
  5. Pair simulation (e.g. Genie) with real robots for scenario breadth before physical deployment.

Edge AI for Smart Cities: From Insight to Action

Smart-city AI that only ships dashboards leaves operators drowning in alerts. The Spectrum/Wiley edge-AI white paper (Intel-sponsored) pushes a next step: cognitive urban systems that turn real-time sensor insight int…

articlecorpus/ieee-spectrum-aicluster/physical-aigap-fill

Keywords: physical-ai-robotics, ieee-spectrum-ai, physical-ai, cluster-physical-ai, corpus-ieee-spectrum-ai, article, gap-fill, edge, smart, cities, from, insight, action

Related: Physical AI / Robotics

Smart-city AI that only ships dashboards leaves operators drowning in alerts. The Spectrum/Wiley edge-AI white paper (Intel-sponsored) pushes a next step: cognitive urban systems that turn real-time sensor insight into local action—at the edge, where latency, bandwidth, and data-sovereignty constraints live. The progression it sketches runs from automation and perception through prediction and agentic coordination to physical AI: infrastructure that continuously perceives, reasons, and acts across public safety, mobility, and infrastructure management.

Historically, city deployments leaned on cameras, sensors, and dashboards that capture data without delivering timely insight. Edge AI changes this by letting inference happen close to where data is generated—supporting faster decisions, stronger data sovereignty, and lower operating costs than cloud-only designs.

Why the edge

City workloads—traffic, safety cameras, utilities—cannot always round-trip to a distant cloud. Edge inference keeps decisions near cameras and controllers, cuts backhaul cost, and can improve privacy by limiting raw video export. The architectural shift is from batch analytics to closed-loop control, with human governance still required for high-stakes acts.

The white paper’s learning outcomes emphasize three practical reasons edge wins for cities:

  • Low-latency decisions when seconds matter for public safety or mobility.
  • Sensitive data kept within city boundaries rather than shipped wholesale to hyperscale regions.
  • Lower dependency on centralized cloud for routine sensing and actuation, with cloud retained for heavier planning.

Computer vision, multimodal sensing, and generative/agentic systems are described as working together—not as competing buzzwords—to support those domains.

Tiered architecture, not “everything on a lamppost”

A useful teaching model is a tiered edge:

  • Far edge — cameras, roadside units, and on-device models for monitoring and immediate reflexes.
  • Regional edge — neighborhood or city-district aggregation for planning and coordination.
  • Cloud — long-horizon analytics, training, and citywide optimization.

Assign monitoring, planning, and action deliberately across tiers; do not collapse every function into one GPU box. Durability, security, and interoperability requirements land on hardware and software alike: unattended cabinets, hostile weather, patch channels that do not brick intersections, and vendors that can coexist.

From insight to actuation

Insight (detect congestion) is not actuation (retime signals). Governance belongs at the act boundary: who may change a light cycle, dispatch a crew, or lock a door, and under what audit trail. Cognitive-city rhetoric fails if “reason and act” skips policy, fail-safes, and human override. Agentic coordination at city scale without exception paths recreates the human-in-the-loop paradox in municipal form.

Design constraints to teach

  • Sensors → on-device/near-device models → policy/action layer → audit logs.
  • Separate insight from actuation; put accountability on the latter.
  • Design for intermittent connectivity and model-update channels that degrade safely.
  • Measure end-to-end latency and failure modes under lost cloud links.
  • Treat data sovereignty as an architecture requirement, not a press-release adjective.
  • Budget for physical AI maintenance: who owns the roadside box when the model drifts?

What “cognitive” must not mean

Cognitive urban systems are not cities that optimize residents without consent. The white paper’s value is architectural—far edge, regional, cloud—plus the reminder that public safety and mobility actions need durable hardware and interoperable software. Pair this article with HITL and governance pieces: municipal agents that retime signals or dispatch crews inherit the same exception-path requirements as enterprise agents. Homework: pick one city workload and mark which decisions may auto-act at the far edge versus which require a human console with an audit log.

Smart-city vendors will pitch “agentic infrastructure.” Demand the tier diagram, the act-boundary policy, and the offline failure mode before the pilot starts.

Sovereignty and cost

Keeping inference local is also a budget story: less raw video egress, fewer surprise cloud bills, and clearer lines about which footage ever leaves city premises. Those are political constraints as much as engineering ones—citizens and councils notice camera pipelines. Edge AI earns trust when it reduces unnecessary centralization, not when it merely relocates the same opaque stack to a cabinet.

Takeaways

  • Edge AI is an operations architecture, not a chip slogan.
  • Cognitive cities need tiered sensing/planning/action—not dashboards alone.
  • Action privileges need the same care as model accuracy.
  • Durability, security, and interoperability decide whether pilots survive year two.
  • Keep cloud for what needs citywide memory; keep reflexes local.

Sources

  • Edge AI for Smart Cities: From Insight to Cognitive Action

Robot Safety When Inputs Lie

IEEE Spectrum AI · Physical AI, Voice & Autonomy · gap-fill/ieee-spectrum-ai/robot-safety-when-inputs-lie.md

Classical robot safety asks whether the machine stays safe when something fails. Physical AI raises a sharper question: can it stay safe when an attacker changes what it sees, hears, or decides—while every safety func…

articlecorpus/ieee-spectrum-aicluster/physical-aigap-fill

Keywords: physical-ai-robotics, ieee-spectrum-ai, physical-ai, cluster-physical-ai, corpus-ieee-spectrum-ai, article, gap-fill, robot, safety, when, inputs

Related: Physical AI / Robotics

Classical robot safety asks whether the machine stays safe when something fails. Physical AI raises a sharper question: can it stay safe when an attacker changes what it sees, hears, or decides—while every safety function still “works”? IEEE Spectrum’s VicOne-sponsored coverage makes the distinction concrete: a robot can obey its rules and still act on a lying world model.

Safety functions vs trusted perception

A mobile robot that slows for a person, a cobot that eases force near a worker, a humanoid that yields space—all depend on distance readings, pose estimates, or stop signals. If those inputs are wrong (fault or deliberate manipulation) and the controller obeys them faithfully, the robot can do the unsafe thing by design: hallway reads clear while someone is there; arm thinks the worker is farther away; stop never arrives.

Compliance with safety rules is not the same as integrity of the sensory and model stack. Independent protective systems still consume readings and messages; if those are poisoned, the “safety layer” may share the lie. VicOne’s framing maps accidental faults and deliberate cyber manipulation onto similar unsafe outcomes so safety and security teams share one threat model.

Attack surface across the stack

Research and lab demos cited across the pieces span layers:

  • Perception / VLA models — adversarial patches that cut task success (arXiv vision-language-action studies); FreezeVLA-style images that cause models to ignore later instructions; poster text treated as a command by a multimodal robot dog (Gemma 4 E4B test); crafted audio inaudible to people changing a hospital-service-robot simulation on Jetson AGX Orin.
  • Training-time backdoors — BadNets-style triggers evolved into BadVLA trajectory hijacks that fire only when a trigger is present while clean performance holds; GoBA reporting high success (cited ~97%) with ordinary objects (e.g., a coffee mug) as triggers.
  • System / middleware — ROS 2/DDS message injection moving a robot organizers expected to stay still under a safe-control setting; UniPwn-style wireless chains with hardcoded keys, auth bypass, command injection, and wormable fleet risk; gyroscope acoustic attacks as a reminder that balance controllers trust sensors (drone research as the classic demonstration).
  • Infrastructure — vulnerabilities that yield root or command injection without “breaking” the safety FSM on paper.

Stealth matters: nothing looks broken while behavior shifts. A model may pass testing yet produce corrupted trajectories when a hidden trigger appears in operation.

What a modern safety program adds

Beyond ISO-style functional safety:

  • Model and vulnerability scanning for Physical AI stacks.
  • Simulation-based validation of corrupted inputs (e.g., NVIDIA Isaac Sim plus adversarial visual tests / VicOne Radeis-style validators) before deployment.
  • Continuous monitoring from development through operation.
  • Test plans that ask “what if the LIDAR/camera/stop channel lies?” with evidence trails.
  • Check whether protective stops depend on the same channels an attacker can spoof.

Fleet wormability turns one compromised unit into an ops crisis—patch cadence and network segmentation belong in the robot safety story, not only in IT ticketing.

Teaching framing

  • Separate functional safety (actuator limits, E-stops) from input integrity.
  • Treat foundation/VLA models as safety-critical components, not app features.
  • Prefer detectable, logged interventions over silent degraded modes.
  • Score Physical AI releases on adversarial simulation results, not only clean-task success.

Independent stops and shared lies

The deepest teaching cut is independence: an E-stop that trusts the same ROS topic an attacker can inject is not independent. BadVLA/GoBA-style triggers that preserve clean accuracy expose validation theater—pass the suite, fail only when the mug appears. Build adversarial sims into release gates; ask whether protective logic has a second sensor path. Homework: for a hallway robot, list every input to “slow for person,” mark which can be spoofed, and propose one cross-check that does not share that channel.

Takeaways

  • Treat perception and foundation models as safety-critical inputs.
  • Validate against malicious and faulty sensor narratives, not only hardware faults.
  • Safety layers that share poisoned channels are not independent.
  • Prefer detectable, logged interventions over silent degraded modes.
  • Backdoors that preserve clean accuracy are a validation blind spot—test triggers on purpose.

Sources

  • Your Robot’s Safety Functions Already Work. What If the Input Lies?
  • Rethinking Robot Safety in the Age of AI

Edge AI: Few-Command Model Bring-Up for Physical Agents

NVIDIA Technical Blog · Physical AI, Voice & Autonomy · gap-fill/nvidia-technical-blog/edge-ai-tensorrt-edge-llm.md

Cabin monitoring, robot perception, and line coordination need models next to sensors. These physical-AI applications must perceive, reason, and act within tight memory, power, and latency budgets. The historical tax…

articlecorpus/nvidia-technical-blogcluster/physical-aigap-fill

Keywords: physical-ai-robotics, nvidia-technical-blog, physical-ai, cluster-physical-ai, corpus-nvidia-technical-blog, article, gap-fill, edge, command, model, bring, physical, agents

Related: Physical AI / Robotics

Cabin monitoring, robot perception, and line coordination need models next to sensors. These physical-AI applications must perceive, reason, and act within tight memory, power, and latency budgets. The historical tax was export/optimize/serve folklore that differed between lab PyTorch and embedded targets. NVIDIA’s TensorRT Edge-LLM path compresses that folklore into a short, repeatable bring-up—prototype on DGX Spark–class boxes, deploy with the same optimized runtime family on the device.

Develop on Spark, deploy with TensorRT Edge-LLM

DGX Spark (including a 64GB configuration) lets embedded teams prototype, fine-tune, and test agents locally. TensorRT Edge-LLM is a lightweight C++ inference runtime aimed at embedded workloads, aligning development on Spark with deployment on platforms such as Jetson Thor, DRIVE AGX Thor, and IGX Thor. The trtedge CLI downloads a chosen model (for example Nemotron-3.5 Lightning NVFP4), builds TensorRT engines, supports terminal prompts and API serving for app prototyping, and can enable speculative decoding (DSpark) for faster generation.

Prerequisites are ordinary but strict: matching CUDA/TensorRT versions (e.g., CUDA 13, TensorRT ≥10.16.1.11 within 10.x) and Python 3.10–3.12. Install into a venv with system site packages so system TensorRT bindings remain visible; verify with a small import that loads the Edge-LLM runtime. First launch downloads the model (~21GB for the Lightning example) and builds engines into ~/.cache/tensorrt-edgellm by default—budget disk. Later launches reuse matching cached engines. The teachable win is a reproducible path from weights to a served local API—not a unique model architecture. Version skew silently recreates the old “works on my laptop” tax.

Local C++ apps beyond the CLI

Companion Do Inference Now (DIN) Deploy samples show how to move from Hugging Face checkpoints to native C++ applications: Python exporters produce ONNX artifacts; C++ CLIs built on ONNX Runtime (with TensorRT RTX execution provider) run shared inference code across Windows and Linux (including Arm64 presets). Vendor-specific CUDA appears only in optional accelerated paths. Samples span ASR (Whisper offline; Parakeet TDT and Nemotron ASR streaming), SAM 2.1 interactive masking, and FLUX.2 image generation with Vulkan/DirectX graphics interop and PTQ via Model Optimizer—quantized ONNX as a drop-in when interfaces stay stable. DGX Spark measurements in the samples show large GPU-vs-CPU speedups (e.g., tens to hundreds of × realtime for selected ASR workloads; SAM 2.1 ~38 FPS GPU vs ~0.5 FPS CPU). The teaching link: Edge-LLM CLI for LLM agents; DIN Deploy for broader local multimodal app patterns on the same class of machines.

Edge still needs agent discipline

A smaller model actuating motors or cameras still needs tool allow-lists, offline fail-safes, and evals on the target power/thermal envelope. Latency and memory on-device are the product constraints; cloud parity is optional. Pair with smart-city edge literacy and robot input-integrity teaching: physical agents inherit both systems and safety constraints. Speculative decoding is a product lever under power limits—measure tokens/sec and watts on the target board, not only on the prototype box.

How to teach edge bring-up

  • Measure tokens/sec and watts on the target board, not only on the prototype box.
  • Treat engine build as a release artifact with pinned versions and cache hygiene.
  • Keep policy hygiene (sandboxes, confirmations) even when the model is small.
  • Prefer few-command CLIs that encode tribal knowledge over wiki sprawl.
  • Separate ONNX export from C++ deployment logic so conversion and app code evolve independently.

Takeaways

  • Edge AI literacy is the bring-up path: one optimized runtime from prototype to device.
  • Speculative decoding and engine builds are product levers under power limits.
  • Agent policy still applies at the edge—small models can still misuse tools.
  • Version-matched stacks beat heroic one-off exports.
  • CLI bring-up (trtedge) and native C++ samples (DIN Deploy / TensorRT RTX) are complementary layers of the same local-AI story.

  • Build Local AI Apps with C++ and NVIDIA TensorRT RTX Samples

Sim-to-Real Robotics: SimReady Assets, Agent Planning, and Policy Training

NVIDIA Technical Blog · Physical AI, Voice & Autonomy · gap-fill/nvidia-technical-blog/robotics-simready-to-real.md

Preparing CAD assets for robotics simulation requires more than converting geometry to OpenUSD: developers must configure and validate materials, collision geometry, joints, and other physics properties before testing…

articlecorpus/nvidia-technical-blogcluster/physical-aigap-fill

Keywords: physical-ai-robotics, nvidia-technical-blog, physical-ai, cluster-physical-ai, corpus-nvidia-technical-blog, article, gap-fill, real, robotics, simready, assets, agent, planning

Related: Physical AI / Robotics

Preparing CAD assets for robotics simulation requires more than converting geometry to OpenUSD: developers must configure and validate materials, collision geometry, joints, and other physics properties before testing robot behavior. A robot model can look correct but still fail in simulation if collision geometry is missing (objects pass through grippers) or joints are wrong (coordinated motion fails). Mass and friction directly affect whether a grasp remains stable. SimReady is the teaching name for that validation gate.

What SimReady means

SimReady defines requirements for preparing OpenUSD assets for specific simulation use cases. Developers select a SimReady profile for their intended use and validate the asset against its requirements. Profile-specific checks validate structure, materials, and physics properties, then flag issues to fix and recheck. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries, guided by SimReady Foundation specifications and agentic NVIDIA skills, provide a structured conversion/validation workflow. Frontier AI models can assist by interpreting reference materials and calling Omniverse tools on the developer’s behalf—reducing manual preparation without removing the need for physics-correct assets.

Five-step asset workflow (YuMi example)

NVIDIA’s walkthrough prepares an ABB Robotics YuMi for simulation with SimReady Foundation and Omniverse tools (GPT-6 Astra cited as one example frontier assistant):

  1. STEP-file conversion into OpenUSD structure.
  2. Appearance validation (materials/looks that matter for perception sims).
  3. Physics configuration — collision geometry, joints, mass, friction, and related properties.
  4. SimReady validation against the chosen profile’s checks.
  5. Task smoke test — e.g., dual-arm pick-and-place with grippers in Isaac Sim.

OpenUSD represents geometry, assembly structure, materials, and simulation properties in a common scene description. The teachable discipline: do not train policies on assets that failed SimReady checks. Pretty renders are not simulation readiness.

Sample inputs for the YuMi walkthrough make the discipline concrete: ABB STEP files as source geometry; reference images/videos to guide appearance and materials; the SimReady Foundation specification repository (also packaged with Isaac Sim 6.1 tier-core) for requirements and validation guidance; and the CAD-to-SimReady skill for conversion, material/physics assignment, and validation. Agents operate Isaac Sim via its remote Python server (windowed mode) so a frontier model can call live simulation APIs—confirm the connection before trusting tool calls. At each step, adapt prompts to the task, then review simulation results and validation feedback; the human still owns physics-correctness sign-off.

From assets to policies and ROS 2

SimReady assets feed Isaac Sim training loops for locomotion and manipulation. Companion posts show AI agents teaching robots (e.g., Microduck-style walk training in simulation) and accelerating ROS 2 nodes with Isaac ROS—bridging planning/perception stacks into the robot software ecosystem. The full sim-to-real literacy stack:

  • World models / generative observation (Cosmos) for sensor diversity.
  • Physics-correct assets (SimReady + Omniverse) for contact fidelity.
  • Policy training in Isaac Sim with held-out eval episodes.
  • Runtime integration via ROS 2 / Isaac ROS for on-robot software.
  • Agent assistants that call tools—not agents that invent physics.

Teaching sim-to-real without magical thinking

  • Separate visual fidelity from physical fidelity; both matter, for different failure modes.
  • Treat SimReady validation as CI for assets—failed checks block policy training jobs.
  • Use agents to operate Omniverse/Isaac tools under profiles; do not let agents skip validation.
  • Measure transfer with systematic domain randomization and real-robot evaluation, not demo videos alone.
  • Keep human review on safety-critical joint limits, collision meshes, and gripper force assumptions.

Takeaways

  • Sim-to-real fails when assets look right but lack collision, joints, mass, or friction—SimReady exists to catch that.
  • Profile-based validation beats ad-hoc “export to USD and hope.”
  • Frontier models help drive Omniverse tools; they do not replace physics specs.
  • Connect SimReady → Isaac training → ROS 2 deployment as one pipeline with gates.
  • Pair with Cosmos world models for observation diversity while keeping physics sim for contact truth.

Do not ship the first generative mesh: SimReady gates and real-robot evals close the loop before claiming sim-to-real success.

Sources

  • Using AI Agents to Teach Robots Like Microduck to Walk in Simulation
  • Accelerating a ROS 2 Node with an AI Agent and NVIDIA Isaac ROS

AI That Designs Chips: Closing the Loop on Silicon

Sequoia · Physical AI, Voice & Autonomy · sequoia/ai-designed-chips.md

Ricursive Intelligence’s founders Anna Goldie and Azalia Mirhoseini represent a recursive bet: use AI to design the chips that run AI. Their Google-era AlphaChip work helped design multiple generations of TPUs and cut chip floor planning from months to hours. The teaching…

articlecorpus/sequoia-ai-knowledgecluster/physical-ai

Keywords: energy-goodput-constraints, ai-designed-chips, sequoia, physical-ai, cluster-physical-ai, corpus-sequoia-ai-knowledge, article, chips, silicon, designs

Related: AI-Designed Chips, Energy & Goodput Constraints

Ricursive Intelligence’s founders Anna Goldie and Azalia Mirhoseini represent a recursive bet: use AI to design the chips that run AI. Their Google-era AlphaChip work helped design multiple generations of TPUs and cut chip floor planning from months to hours. The teaching core is not “RL cool demos”—it is closing the loop between learned placement and the painful constraints of real tapeout, then accelerating design until models and hardware can co-evolve.

Definition: AI-for-EDA vs proxy optimization

Chip design is a multi-year, often hundreds-of-millions-of-dollars bottleneck. Floor planning places macros and logic so wire length, timing, power, and manufacturability work together. AI that designs chips means learned systems proposing placements (and, broader, design decisions) inside or beside real EDA flows—not academic sketches that never meet a signoff timer.

The product lesson generalizes beyond EDA: if your reward function is not the real objective, RL will optimize the wrong world. Academic proxies such as half-perimeter wire length can look publishable and still anger chip designers who live in timing closure, power, congestion, and tool-flow reality. Successful work sits inside the real toolchain, with rewards defined by engineers who ship silicon—not only by papers.

AlphaChip-era results included unusual “alien” placements (curved and donut-like patterns) that reduced wire length, power, and timing violations—move-37 moments human designers would hesitate to try. Novelty is valuable only when the fab and signoff stack agree.

Mechanism: from fabless to designless, and co-design

Goldie and Mirhoseini describe an industry shift analogy: TSMC enabled fabless giants; Ricursive aims at designless—companies creating custom silicon without maintaining enormous in-house design teams. Asymmetric cycles today hurt co-design: AI methods evolve faster than chips can be built. Compressing design time unlocks true co-evolution of workloads, applications, and silicon—the recursive self-improvement loop where better chips train better design models that propose better chips.

Synthetic data and large-scale training on placement/design distributions matter because real tapeouts are scarce. The mechanism is not a single magic net; it is models + EDA integration + feedback from timing/power/manufacturability oracles that approximate what tapeout cares about.

Dylan Patel / SemiAnalysis themes sharpen why this matters for AI companies: hardware–software co-design is framed as a real 100× lever—not a slogan. Model sparsity and density pull toward different accelerators; teams shaped for one GPU generation struggle on another; memory bandwidth (HBM stacks today, tighter on-package memory tomorrow) dominates what algorithms can afford. CUDA’s “moat” is less a language trick than a full stack of libraries, kernels, and ecosystem. If AI shortens chip design and software is co-tuned, the cost curve of intelligence bends again—alongside energy and data-efficiency work.

Why chip design is the AI bottleneck

Neural nets existed for decades; they became practical when compute did. If chips remain the slow, expensive constraint, scaling laws stall on fabrication calendars. AI that proposes better floorplans and, eventually, broader design automation, attacks that bottleneck from inside the loop—especially for custom accelerators matched to real training and inference graphs.

Failure modes

  • Proxy reward theater. Optimizing HPWL (or any single metric) while timing/power regress in the real flow.
  • Paper-only EDA. Methods that cannot sit in production toolchains or that designers refuse to trust.
  • Ignoring manufacturability. Beautiful placements that will not yield.
  • Co-design theater. Buying GPUs while treating model architecture as hardware-agnostic forever—then wondering why a sparse expert model hates your accelerator.
  • Cycle mismatch. Assuming software can wait years for the “perfect” chip without intermediate co-optimization.
  • Talent myth. Believing designless means zero chip expertise; you still need people who can define rewards, constraints, and signoff.

Practices for AI builders (even if you never tape out)

Treat reward design as product management: write the real objective (latency at batch size B, $/token, joules/token, yield) and refuse proxies that diverge. Prefer co-design checklists when choosing model shapes (sparsity, precision, memory traffic). Track goodput and bandwidth, not only peak FLOPs. If you use learned autosystems (compilers, schedulers, placement), demand ablation against the metrics ops will fire you for.

Practice checklist

  • Name the true objective (timing, power, $/token, joules) before choosing a learning reward; document proxy gaps.
  • Integrate learned tools into the real EDA or compiler flow early—refuse offline-only demos as launch criteria.
  • Include designer-in-the-loop review for trust and constraint capture; measure override rates.
  • Use synthetic + historical design data deliberately; watch distribution shift vs your next node/process.
  • For model↔chip co-design: match sparsity/density and memory traffic to the target accelerator family.
  • Budget for iteration speed (hours/days vs months) as a first-class roadmap goal—slow loops kill co-evolution.
  • Prefer full-stack evaluation (libraries, kernels, interconnect) over single-kernel peaks when claiming speedups.
  • If pursuing “designless” custom silicon, still staff constraint owners who can say no to unsafe proposals.

Sources

  • AI That Designs Its Own Chips: Ricursive's Anna Goldie and Azalia Mirhoseini
  • How Ricursive Intelligence’s Founders are Using AI to Shape The Future of Chip Design
  • Why Hardware-Software Co-Design Is AI's Real 100x: Dylan Patel of SemiAnalysis

Autonomy at Scale: Reliability Is the Product

Sequoia · Physical AI, Voice & Autonomy · sequoia/autonomy-at-scale.md

Waymo’s Dmitri Dolgov (20M+ fully autonomous rides), Zipline’s long-distance delivery record (on the order of 140M miles with a zero-incident framing in their Training Data conversation), and Wayve’s end-to-end “AV 2.0” story converge on one teaching point: in the physical…

articlecorpus/sequoia-ai-knowledgecluster/physical-ai

Keywords: physical-ai---robotics, autonomy-reliability, sequoia, physical-ai, cluster-physical-ai, corpus-sequoia-ai-knowledge, article, reliability, product, autonomy

Related: Autonomy Reliability, Physical AI - Robotics

Waymo’s Dmitri Dolgov (20M+ fully autonomous rides), Zipline’s long-distance delivery record (on the order of 140M miles with a zero-incident framing in their Training Data conversation), and Wayve’s end-to-end “AV 2.0” story converge on one teaching point: in the physical world, reliability engineering eats model demos. Autonomy that scales is less “watch the neural net drive” and more closed loops of data, simulation, operational design domains, and organizations that treat incidents as learning systems.

Definition: autonomy vs demo autonomy

Autonomy at scale means a system repeatedly completes real work—rides, deliveries, drives—without a safety driver in the loop for the marketed ODD, at volumes where rare events dominate risk. Demo autonomy completes a curated route once. The gap is statistical: fleets accumulate edge cases that never appear in a launch video.

Waymo’s public scaling numbers make the phase change concrete: over 20 million fully autonomous rides, with a large fraction arriving in a short recent window; multi-city launches in a day; years to early mileage milestones, then rapid multiplication. Zipline’s arc—from blood delivery in Rwanda when U.S. drone delivery was still illegal, toward commercial partnerships and a cost curve that fell dramatically per delivery—shows autonomy as a logistics system, not a flying camera. Wayve argues end-to-end learning can generalize across cities without HD-map absolutism—but public trust still rides on measured safety, not architecture branding.

Mechanism: loops, pillars, and systems around the vehicle

Waymo describes a foundation-model core powering three pillars: the driver, the simulator, and the critic—related but distinct tasks that need world physics, good-driving norms, and evaluation of action effects. They are clear that “end-to-end” (sensors toward actions in one learned system) is not the same as purely relying on a vanilla end-to-end stack for superhuman safety at hundreds of millions of miles. Learned representations are augmented with structured materialization—maps, policies, and engineering layers—so deployment gates are not “the net felt confident.”

Zipline’s teaching mechanism is harsher: the drone itself is only about 15% of the solution. The rest is inventory management, air traffic integration, and safety engineering such as dual flight-computer failover that can save a delivery mid-flight. Reliability is not “ask the supplier for an MTBF”; if you are the supplier of the full system, you own the stack. Weather includes weird cases like solar weather degrading GPS via the ionosphere—ODD is physics, not a city polygon alone.

Wayve’s AV 2.0 mechanism pushes generalization-first end-to-end learning: adapt to new vehicles and cities in weeks, train across countries and sensor setups, use world models for complex reasoning, partner with OEMs for scale beyond robotaxis. The complement to Waymo’s caution is speed of transfer; the shared requirement is evidence before expansion.

What actually scales

  • Continuous data closed-loops from the fleet into training, simulation, and critique.
  • Conservative ODD that expands with evidence, plus local community and operational work when opening cities.
  • Organizations that instrument failures for process change—not only model fine-tunes.
  • Layered stacks: learned components plus maps/simulation/policy where needed; avoid “end-to-end or bust” absolutism in deployment rhetoric.
  • Cost and ops centers as product: Zipline’s path toward cheaper-than-a-car delivery implies autonomy economics, not only autonomy demos.

Failure modes

  • Research milestones sold as deployment gates. A successful closed-course run is not a city launch.
  • Vanilla end-to-end in production. Insufficient alone for extreme safety at fleet scale without structured augmentation and critics.
  • Vehicle-only thinking. Ignoring inventory, ATC, failover, and update cadence (how long does a legacy OEM take to ship software?).
  • ODD hand-waving. “Mostly sunny suburbs” without solar, RF, weather, and human-behavior tails.
  • Incident PR over learning systems. If postmortems do not change training and process, scale amplifies the same failure.
  • Architecture tribalism. Map-heavy vs map-light debates that ignore measured outcomes in the target ODD.

Practice checklist

  • Define ODD explicitly (geography, weather, speed, road types, connectivity) and list expansion evidence required.
  • Instrument every failure for training data, simulation coverage, and process change—with owners.
  • Separate research milestones from deployment gates; require critic/simulation pass rates before widening ODD.
  • Budget ops centers, failover, and update pipelines as core COGS—not “support.”
  • Prefer fleet closed-loops over one-off demo routes when prioritizing eng work.
  • For embodied agents: decide where learned policy ends and hard constraints / structured state begin.
  • Track cost per successful mission alongside model metrics; autonomy that cannot clear unit economics will not stay scaled.
  • When adopting end-to-end learning, still publish how you evaluate safety beyond average-case driving score.

Sources

  • Inside Zipline's Autonomous System: 140M Miles, Zero Incidents

Robot Data Factories: Sensorizing Humans to Train Physical AI

Sequoia · Physical AI, Voice & Autonomy · sequoia/robot-data-factories.md

Language models pretrain on the internet. Robotics has no equivalent corpus. Sequoia’s conversations with Mecka’s Josh Gao, NVIDIA’s Jim Fan, Physical Intelligence’s Karol Hausman and Tobi Springenberg, and Hugging Face’s Thomas Wolf converge on a manufacturing problem: how…

articlecorpus/sequoia-ai-knowledgecluster/physical-ai

Keywords: physical-ai---robotics, data-efficiency-bottleneck, sequoia, physical-ai, cluster-physical-ai, corpus-sequoia-ai-knowledge, article, physical, data, robot

Related: Data Efficiency Bottleneck, Physical AI - Robotics

Language models pretrain on the internet. Robotics has no equivalent corpus. Sequoia’s conversations with Mecka’s Josh Gao, NVIDIA’s Jim Fan, Physical Intelligence’s Karol Hausman and Tobi Springenberg, and Hugging Face’s Thomas Wolf converge on a manufacturing problem: how to produce physical experience at scale—and then distribute skills the way software platforms distribute apps.

Definition: what a robot data factory is

A robot data factory is an industrial system for creating, cleaning, and licensing the multimodal trajectories that train physical AI: pixels (what the world looks like from an embodied POV), actions (how bodies move and grasp), and logic (task structure and success criteria). Gao’s Mecka thesis is blunt: robotics is data-constrained in a way LLMs were not. The cold start is not free web text; it is paid collection, sensorized humans, partner sites, and quality gates.

Egocentric data—first-person video of humans demonstrating tasks—is a core feedstock. Robots experience the world from a POV; showing them human POV closes much of the vision gap even before you solve full embodiment transfer. Earlier egocentric corpora (Gao cites Ego4D-scale collections on the order of thousands of hours) proved the format but often captured daily life rather than task-complete industrial trajectories. A factory’s job is to make the distribution match what policies need: diverse, labeled, success-complete work—not bowling highlight reels.

Mechanism: from human sensing to generalist robots

Think of the stack in layers.

1. Capture hardware and ops. Wearables and sensorized humans turn people into temporary robots—recording rich demonstration without waiting for a perfect humanoid fleet. Ops matter as much as sensors: which tasks, which environments, which worker partners, and which quality gates decide whether a take enters training.

2. Multimodal warehousing. Trajectories must stay aligned across video, proprioception/actions, and task metadata. “Lots of video” without action labels and success flags is a content library, not a training factory.

3. Foundation models for the physical world. Fan’s NVIDIA GEAR framing describes a three-pronged data strategy—internet-scale priors, simulation, and real robot data—aiming at a foundation agent that generalizes across skills, embodiments, and even physical vs. virtual realities. Historical LLM pattern he emphasizes: specialists first, then generalists, then specialized generalists (prompt/fine-tune/distill the generalist back onto a task)—and the specialized generalist usually wins. Robotics is still climbing toward that generalist moment across embodiments.

Physical Intelligence states the endgame explicitly: robotic foundation models that, in principle, let any robot do any task. Their claim is that robotics has been held back less by hardware than by an intelligence bottleneck foundation models can attack—end-to-end learning of generalizable behavior rather than task-specific programs, with real-world deployment and RL-from-experience to push past pure imitation.

4. Distribution layer. Wolf’s Hugging Face angle is platform economics: once basic building blocks exist, an “app store” dynamic for robot skills and physical AI components can emerge—open distribution of models, datasets, and tools so builders compose rather than recreate the stack. Data remains the bottleneck; openness is a bet that shared infrastructure accelerates everyone the way Hub ecosystems accelerated NLP.

Constraints unique to physical AI

  • No free pretraining dump. Every useful hour is expensive; commercial unlocks (simple pick-and-place first, then the long tail) pace the economically feasible scale.
  • Embodiment and sim-to-real gaps. Simulation helps (Fan highlights NVIDIA’s graphics advantage and even LLMs writing reward functions for self-play), but transfer still bites.
  • Safety has physical consequences. Failed policies bruise people and property, not just reputation scores.
  • Social and rights friction. Workplace instrumentation, worker consent, and data licensing are load-bearing product decisions—not afterthoughts.
  • Long-tail task diversity. The easy demos are not the economy; Gao notes the long tail is orders of magnitude larger than early unlocks.

Failure modes

  • Robot SKUs before data ops. Buying arms without a capture → warehouse → train → redeploy loop.
  • Internet-video cosplay. Scraping third-person web video and calling it robotics pretraining without action/logic alignment.
  • Demo theater. One-off teleop videos that do not survive distribution shift across sites, lighting, objects, or operators.
  • Specialist dead ends. Shipping a narrow picker that cannot absorb a foundation-model upgrade path (Fan’s warning: specialists are easier short-term; generalists unlock the compounding loop).
  • Ignoring the platform layer. Training a closed skill with no path to share, version, or compose—then rediscovering Hugging Face-style distribution pain later.
  • Underfunding quality gates. Volume without curation teaches robots the wrong world.

Practice checklist

  • Design data capture (sensors, consent, task taxonomy) before scaling robot SKUs
  • Prefer tasks with crisp success criteria so imitation and RL get a real learning signal
  • Budget continuous data ops—collection, labeling, relicensing—not a one-off demo sprint
  • Mix internet priors, sim, and real trajectories deliberately; measure sim-to-real failure explicitly
  • Separate fleet reliability engineering from model research early (broken robots poison data and trust)
  • Plan for specialized-generalist fine-tunes once a generalist base exists—don’t only accumulate one-off specialists
  • Treat open distribution (datasets, policies, evals) as a growth loop if you want an “app store” ecosystem
  • Instrument data rights and workplace policy as part of the ML pipeline, not as legal cleanup
